Because this tactic equips the threat, findings here warrant faster escalation than the earlier target-development tactics, and any finding correlating with surveillance, rehearsal, or staging behavior elsewhere warrants immediate response-protocol activation regardless of this tactic's internal tier. Multiple lower-tier findings correlating in time or toward one attack means compose to a higher aggregate tier than any one warrants alone; consumer triage tooling should make this composition rule explicit. Tier-triggered actions: the monitoring tier triggers logging and pattern-detection; the investigation tier triggers actor identification, a capability assessment, and a review of the subject's exposure; the elevation tier triggers a structured threat assessment, subject-protective measures, and law-enforcement liaison; the committed-actor tier triggers defensive-posture coordination and urgent law-enforcement engagement.

tactics.name: Network Development
tactics.notes: Recruiting and organizing facilitators, access agents, cutouts, and handlers who will support the operation. Network development converts a solo actor into a multi-node threat with distributed capabilities and deniability. For lone actors, this tactic may be absent — its absence is itself an indicator of actor type.
tactics.cpn_notes: Encrypted messaging apps, dark web forums, and privacy-preserving communications platforms are the coordination infrastructure for modern operational networks. Recruitment can occur entirely online with no physical meeting before execution.

indicators.behavior: Threat actor introduces another individual to the grievance narrative through shared communications, joint research, or coordinated complaint
Threat actor begins coordinating logistics, schedules, or transportation with another individual whose involvement is operationally relevant rather than socially incidental
Threat actor communicates with peers, online associates, or co-ideologues in a forum or platform that openly endorses violence or targeted harm
Threat actor recruits or attempts to recruit family members, employees, or social connections to provide access, transportation, capability, or information about the targeted subject
Threat actor transfers attack-relevant information — target details, schedule, environmental data, capability — to another individual via written or verbal communication
Threat actor's pattern of contact shifts to include new associates whose connection has no clear social or professional basis, particularly in a compressed time window

countermeasures.measure: Maintain insider-threat program coverage of association patterns including new co-worker affiliations, off-hours coordination, and out-of-band communication channels
countermeasures.limitations: Personal associations are protected information; programs must be scoped to job-relevant context. False-positive rate is high without behavioral baseline

countermeasures.measure: Deliver awareness briefings for associates of the targeted subject — coworkers, family members, friends — on common recruitment patterns including requests to provide access, transportation, or information that seems unrelated to legitimate need
countermeasures.limitations: Recruitment requests may be subtle or framed as personal favors. Effectiveness depends on the associate's ability to recognize the pattern in retrospect

countermeasures.measure: Conduct open-source and authorized closed-source intelligence collection on online forums and platforms known to host content that endorses violence or coordinates targeted harm against individuals, mapping participants to organizational interest where appropriate
countermeasures.limitations: Most participants in such forums are not operationally relevant; analyst time is the binding constraint. Privacy and platform-policy considerations require careful scoping

countermeasures.measure: Establish reporting expectations across the workforce for unusual coordination requests, recruitment overtures, or off-band communications that touch organizationally sensitive information
countermeasures.limitations: Reporting culture matures slowly; many concerning requests are dismissed as harmless when received

response_protocols.trigger: Single Network Development indicator reported (recruitment overture, unusual co-coordination, joint grievance escalation)
response_protocols.action: Document the indicator. Conduct a 5-business-day preliminary assessment that includes (a) corroboration of the observation, (b) baseline review of the threat actor's recent association patterns, (c) identification of the recruited individual or associate. Determine whether the association is operationally relevant or socially incidental.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Association determined operationally relevant OR concurrent indicators surface from another Phase 1 tactic.
response_protocols.legal_notes: Investigation of personal associations carries privacy implications; coordinate with legal before any inquiry beyond the immediate observation. Document factually. This guidance does not constitute legal advice. Consult qualified legal counsel for jurisdiction-specific requirements.

response_protocols.trigger: Multiple Network Development indicators co-observed for the same threat actor OR confirmed transfer of attack-relevant information OR confirmed recruitment of an associate to provide access or capability
response_protocols.action: Convene the threat management team. Conduct full risk assessment including the recruited associate's risk profile. Brief protective operations on the expanded threat surface (now multi-node). Coordinate with HR if an associate is an employee; coordinate with law enforcement if recruitment crosses into criminal conspiracy.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Multi-node coordination demonstrates means and proximity to targeted subject OR confirmed planning across the network.
response_protocols.legal_notes: Conspiracy thresholds and reporting obligations vary materially by jurisdiction. Document the indicator constellation that drove escalation including evidence of coordination beyond mere association. Preserve evidence. This guidance does not constitute legal advice. Consult qualified legal counsel for jurisdiction-specific requirements.

tactics.field_notes: By the time Network Development is observable, the threat actor has decided they need help — co-conspirators for execution, witting or unwitting accomplices for capability acquisition, or supporters for ideological reinforcement. The introduction of a second voice into the grievance narrative is the first detectable shift. Once that voice is present, an investigator can usually find concrete artifacts: shared communications, joint research, transferred information, and sometimes a meeting cadence that did not exist before. Network Development can be small (one accomplice for transportation) or large (a cell organized around a shared ideology). The work for the analyst is distinguishing connection that is operationally relevant from connection that is socially incidental. The absence of Network Development in a developing case is itself diagnostic — it signals the threat actor is preparing as a lone operator and the case will likely not produce coordination artifacts.
observed_contexts: workplace violence case where the threat actor recruited a coworker to provide after-hours building access in exchange for help with personal grievances unrelated to the attack

domestic case where the threat actor's pattern of contact shifted in the weeks before mobilization to include a new associate met online whose role in the attack was not understood until after-action review
extremist case where co-ideologue communications in an encrypted group preceded coordinated capability acquisition by months

Across casework, insider actors building target access often work through people already in their orbit — co-workers, family members, professional contacts drawn in to extend access without drawing scrutiny
lone-actor case where the absence of any associate involvement was itself diagnostic; the threat assessment team correctly anticipated a single-actor execution

tactics.name: Cover Construction
tactics.notes: Building a false identity or pretext that explains the actor's presence near the subject without raising suspicion. Cover construction ranges from a minimal behavioral pretext (posing as a jogger) to a full legend (fabricated identity with verifiable history).
tactics.cpn_notes: Synthetic social media presence, forged digital credentials, and fake email and phone infrastructure are standard components of modern cover identity construction. A digital footprint is now an expected component of a credible legend.

indicators.behavior: Threat actor adopts an identity, uniform, or vehicle marking inconsistent with their actual employment, education, or background
Threat actor presents fabricated credentials — employer ID, contractor badge, business cards, vendor identification — when seeking access to restricted environments
Threat actor establishes shell social media profiles, online personas, or business presence to support a cover identity used for approach or surveillance
Threat actor's stated reason for being at a location does not align with verifiable activity — no work order, no scheduled appointment, no destination, no sponsoring contact

Threat actor's verbal account of their role contains gaps inconsistent with someone actually in that role — wrong jargon, missing routine knowledge, cannot answer basic procedural questions someone working that job day-to-day would know
Threat actor's identifying details — name, employer, license plate, business name — cannot be corroborated through normal verification channels

countermeasures.measure: Enforce visitor verification protocols requiring confirmable work orders, scheduled appointments, or sponsoring contact before access to restricted environments
countermeasures.limitations: Verification fatigue erodes effectiveness during high-traffic periods; sophisticated threat actors pre-stage sponsoring contacts that withstand basic verification

countermeasures.measure: Train reception and security personnel on second-order identity verification — challenge questions about role-specific knowledge, procedural details, and routine artifacts the cover identity should possess
countermeasures.limitations: Personnel may default to politeness over challenge; effectiveness depends on culture that empowers reception staff to question

countermeasures.measure: Pre-coordinate supplier and vendor visits including verified contact lookup, expected arrival window, and named individuals authorized to attend
countermeasures.limitations: Pre-coordination overhead can slow legitimate operations; emergency or unscheduled visits create gaps in coverage

countermeasures.measure: Implement two-factor identity verification for sensitive area access — visual badge plus sponsoring-contact callback or biometric, with escort requirements for unverified visitors
countermeasures.limitations: Cost and friction grow with sensitivity tier; insider sponsors can defeat callback verification if not separately validated

response_protocols.trigger: Single Cover Construction indicator detected (unverifiable identity claim, fabricated credentials, role-knowledge incongruity reported by reception or peer)
response_protocols.action: Document the indicator. Detain politely if the individual is on-site; verify identity through sponsoring contact or external corroboration. Report to threat management team within the same business day. Preserve any physical artifacts (business cards, IDs, vehicle photos).
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Identity cannot be corroborated OR cover artifact connects to other concerning context (prior surveillance reports, prior access attempts).
response_protocols.legal_notes: Detention or extended challenge of an individual carries legal implications that vary by jurisdiction. Coordinate with legal before any action beyond polite verification. Document factually; do not characterize the individual's intent. This guidance does not constitute legal advice. Consult qualified legal counsel for jurisdiction-specific requirements.

response_protocols.trigger: Cover construction detected at access to a sensitive area OR concurrent with other Phase 1 indicators OR coupled with proximity to the targeted subject
response_protocols.action: Activate full incident response. Detain pending verification where lawful. Notify law enforcement; pretexting at protected sites may itself be unlawful. Implement enhanced posture for the targeted subject and the affected facility. Capture all physical and digital evidence of the cover construction.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Cover construction breaches a sensitive perimeter OR threat actor flees on challenge OR identity ties to prior threat case.
response_protocols.legal_notes: Pretexting and trespass laws vary; some jurisdictions criminalize cover construction at protected sites independently of intent. Preserve evidence carefully. This guidance does not constitute legal advice. Consult qualified legal counsel for jurisdiction-specific requirements.

tactics.field_notes: The thing about Cover Construction is that it doesn't usually fail at the cover — it fails at the second-order detail nobody scripted: the wrong jargon for the role, a missing employer-issued artifact, a procedure that does not match the claimed credential, or knowledge gaps an actual member of that role would not have. A threat actor with a 'utility worker' cover may have the uniform but no work order, no truck, and no answer for which substation they're servicing. An investigator catches Cover Construction by interrogating the second order: not 'is this person who they claim to be?' but 'do their answers, artifacts, and behavior match the role they claim?' The signal is small mismatches between the claimed identity and the operational details only someone actually working that role would know. Cover Construction can range from a minimal behavioral pretext (posing as a jogger or rideshare passenger) to a full legend (fabricated identity with verifiable employer history and online footprint), and the detection difficulty rises in proportion.
observed_contexts: executive protection case where a threat actor in a contractor uniform was challenged at reception; the work order did not exist and the truck in the parking lot belonged to a different vendor
stalking case where the threat actor maintained a fabricated dating-app persona for months to support repeated approach attempts on the targeted subject
insider-conspirator case where an external accomplice presented forged contractor credentials in coordination with an insider sponsor who validated the cover

Vendor or contractor identity is the dominant cover-for-action pattern across facility-targeted casework — fabricated business presence supported by visible artifacts (badge requests, scheduled deliveries, accompanied walkthroughs) that precede any kinetic action
domestic case where a low-tech behavioral cover (jogger, dog walker) sustained repeated environmental survey of the targeted subject's residence over several weeks

tactics.name: Pathway Indicators
tactics.notes: Observable pre-attack behavioral signals — grievance escalation, ideation, leakage, and preparation behaviors — that indicate an actor is moving toward violence. For fixated individuals and insider threats, pathway indicators are often the only pre-attack detection window. These are not tactics the actor chooses to execute; they are behavioral byproducts of the threat development process detectable by protective intelligence practitioners.
tactics.cpn_notes: Online leakage via social media posts, forum activity, messaging apps, and blog content is now the most detectable pre-attack indicator channel. Digital leakage often occurs before physical preparation begins and may continue throughout the threat development cycle.

indicators.behavior: Threat actor exhibits ideation behavior — referencing violent solutions to grievance, romanticizing prior attackers, or framing harm to the targeted subject as the only viable path forward
Threat actor moves from generalized statements of harm to specific planning behavior — selecting a method, identifying timing, evaluating opportunities for access to the targeted subject
Threat actor engages in preparation behavior — acquiring weapons, conducting dry runs, surveilling locations, or making logistical arrangements consistent with an attack plan
Threat actor exhibits a final-act behavioral signature — distributing personal possessions, writing a manifesto, recording a final statement, or saying goodbye to a confidant

Threat actor exhibits identification with prior attackers — collecting media coverage of past incidents, studying tradecraft details, or expressing admiration for individuals who have committed targeted violence
Threat actor exhibits a discrete escalation in the kind or intensity of violent imagery, statement, or low-level act distinct from the threat actor's prior behavioral baseline
Threat actor exhibits a sudden visible increase in goal-directed activity such as research, communication, movement, or expenditure consistent with imminent action

countermeasures.measure: Train the threat management team and security peer reporters on the eight pathway warning signs (per Meloy TRAP-18 / Calhoun-Weston pathway model) so concerning behaviors are recognized at the pattern level rather than as isolated events
countermeasures.limitations: Pathway literacy fades without periodic refresh; novel aggression and energy burst signals are particularly difficult to distinguish from baseline at low frequency

countermeasures.measure: Establish a structured behavioral assessment workflow that maps observed indicators to pathway stages (ideation, planning, preparation, breach, attack), with explicit escalation gates at each stage
countermeasures.limitations: Stage assignment requires trained judgment; pathway progression is not strictly linear and can compress under pressure or skip stages entirely in some case typologies

countermeasures.measure: Implement organizational reporting culture that captures pre-attack signals at low thresholds, including peer reports of concerning statements, fixation behaviors, and behavioral baseline shifts, without retaliation against reporters
countermeasures.limitations: Effectiveness depends on organizational trust and reporting maturity; many pre-attack signals are dismissed by associates as 'just talk' until corroborated by other indicators

countermeasures.measure: Conduct retrospective pathway analysis on prior threat assessment cases (closed and active) to validate that the framework distinguishes pathway progression from baseline behavior in the operational environment
countermeasures.limitations: Retrospective analysis is subject to hindsight bias; pathway-stage determinations made after a known outcome may not generalize cleanly to live cases

response_protocols.trigger: One or more pathway indicators detected at ideation or research stage for an identified threat actor, alone or in combination with other Phase 1 tactic indicators
response_protocols.action: Document each indicator against the pathway model. Conduct behavioral baseline review for the threat actor. Determine pathway stage (ideation / planning / preparation / breach / attack). Open or update the case file. Brief the threat management team within 5 business days. Establish a monitoring cadence appropriate to the assigned pathway stage.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Pathway progresses from ideation to planning OR concurrent indicators surface from another Phase 1 tactic for the same threat actor.
response_protocols.legal_notes: Pathway-stage determinations are protective intelligence assessments, not clinical or psychiatric findings — document them as observable behavior patterns, not mental health characterizations. If the threat actor is an employee, coordinate with HR before any direct engagement. This guidance does not constitute legal advice. Consult qualified legal counsel for jurisdiction-specific requirements.

response_protocols.trigger: Pathway indicators reach preparation stage (means acquisition, dry runs, logistical staging) OR a final-act behavioral signature is observed OR an energy burst is detected concurrent with prior pathway indicators
response_protocols.action: Convene the threat management team within 24 hours. Conduct formal threat assessment using structured professional judgment. Implement protective measures for the targeted subject including awareness brief, posture increase, and route variation. Initiate enhanced monitoring of the threat actor across available data sources. Coordinate with law enforcement; consider interdiction options if jurisdiction permits.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Threat actor demonstrates means and proximity to the targeted subject OR direct or indirect threat communicated OR breach attempt observed.
response_protocols.legal_notes: At preparation stage and beyond, parallel notifications to legal and (when applicable) law enforcement become standard. Document the indicator constellation that drove escalation — particularly the pathway-stage rationale — and preserve evidence of the original observations. Consult counsel on jurisdiction-specific reporting obligations and on privileged-communication scope for the threat management team. This guidance does not constitute legal advice.

tactics.field_notes: Pathway Indicators are the observable behaviors that mark a threat actor's progression toward an attack — grievance escalation, ideation, leakage, planning, preparation, and the final-act behaviors that often appear in the days or hours before mobilization. The pathway is described in the literature as a sequence of stages (Calhoun-Weston: ideation → research → planning → preparation → breach → attack; Meloy's TRAP-18 codifies the proximal warning signs). In casework, an analyst rarely observes every stage in order — what surfaces is a few signals from different stages, and the work is mapping those signals against the pathway model to locate the threat actor at a specific stage with a specific time horizon. The most catchable signals tend to be ideation (in writing or peer-reported speech), preparation (means acquisition shows up in financial or procurement records), and the energy burst right before action. The recurring detection failure is not absence of signal — it is failure to aggregate scattered signals across reporters and recognize them as pathway.
observed_contexts: [literature: MELOY-TRAP18-2016 / FEIN-VOSSEKUIL-1999 — consensus pattern of ideation-to-action progression preceding targeted attacks by weeks to months]
[literature: NTAC-MASS-2021 — pre-attack warning behaviors documented in the majority of mass attacks against public spaces]
[literature: FBI-PREATTACK-2018 — concerning behaviors observed by associates and family members during the months preceding active shooter attacks]
workplace violence case with documented progression from generalized grievance to specific planning to means acquisition over a six-month window
domestic terrorism investigation where peer-reported ideation and online identification with prior attackers preceded weapons acquisition by months

tactics.name: Surveillance Detection Countermeasures
tactics.notes: Actor takes deliberate actions to detect whether they are under protective intelligence or law enforcement surveillance. The presence of this behavior signals operational sophistication and awareness of protective programs. Detection of counter-surveillance attempts is itself a high-confidence indicator of a developing threat.
tactics.cpn_notes: Digital counter-surveillance includes checking devices for surveillance software, monitoring social media for mentions of their name or image, and using RF detection apps to identify surveillance equipment. Sophisticated actors may monitor protective intelligence social media accounts for indicators of active investigation.

indicators.behavior: Threat actor varies vehicle, route, or arrival time across repeated visits to a targeted-subject-associated location in a pattern consistent with deliberate surveillance detection
Threat actor performs vehicle dismounts and walking transitions at non-destination points (parking-lot-to-walking pattern, ride-share-then-walk) before arriving at the actual location of interest
Threat actor uses cutouts, intermediaries, or third parties for tasks that would normally be performed directly — calling, visiting, or asking questions about the targeted subject's environment
Threat actor substitutes physical reconnaissance with technical surrogates — satellite imagery, Street View, public live cameras, drone overflight — to avoid being physically observed at the location
Threat actor uses VPN, Tor, burner devices, anonymous accounts, or pseudonymous social media to mask digital reconnaissance activity directed at the targeted subject or environment
Threat actor maintains a thin cover story for proximity to the target environment that they activate only when challenged or observed, distinct from the routine cover used for active access attempts

countermeasures.measure: Train surveillance detection sweeps to recognize over-engineered variance — repeated minor changes to a recurring observation pattern that exceed organic schedule diversity
countermeasures.limitations: Distinguishing over-engineered variance from organic schedule diversity is judgment-intensive; false positive rate is high without trained operators

countermeasures.measure: Implement multi-camera correlation across non-adjacent observation points — matching faces, vehicles, or behavioral signatures across approach routes to detect cutout patterns and walking transitions
countermeasures.limitations: Cross-camera correlation requires coverage density and either operator time or analytics support; privacy considerations apply outside controlled environments

countermeasures.measure: Maintain network-level monitoring for access from anonymized IP ranges, Tor exit nodes, or pseudonymous services to high-value internal resources associated with the targeted subject
countermeasures.limitations: Anonymizing services have legitimate uses; alerting must be tuned to context to avoid noise. Sophisticated threat actors will rotate anonymizing infrastructure

countermeasures.measure: Conduct random-interval rotations of surveillance detection observation positions, vehicles, and personnel to defeat threat-actor pattern modeling of the protective surveillance team itself
countermeasures.limitations: Rotations create coverage gaps if not coordinated; sophisticated threat actors may infer the rotation schedule itself given enough observations

response_protocols.trigger: Single Surveillance Detection Countermeasure indicator detected (over-engineered variance, walking transition, cutout pattern, technical-surrogate reconnaissance)
response_protocols.action: Document the indicator. Conduct a 5-business-day preliminary assessment that includes (a) corroboration through additional observation, (b) cross-camera or multi-source correlation where available, (c) baseline review of any threat actor candidate. SD-CM behavior is itself a high-confidence signal of operational sophistication; treat the detection threshold accordingly.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: SD-CM activity confirmed across multiple observation points OR concurrent with other Phase 1 indicators.
response_protocols.legal_notes: Detection of SD-CM behavior raises the inferred sophistication of the threat actor and may justify enhanced monitoring within legal scope. Document the basis for any escalation. This guidance does not constitute legal advice. Consult qualified legal counsel for jurisdiction-specific requirements.

response_protocols.trigger: Multiple SD-CM indicators co-observed for the same threat actor OR SD-CM behavior coupled with confirmed environmental survey or capability acquisition
response_protocols.action: Convene the threat management team. Treat SD-CM presence as evidence of operational sophistication. Implement enhanced protective posture including SD team rotation and coverage tightening. Coordinate with law enforcement to share the SD-CM signature; an externally-coordinated threat actor may be in scope of broader investigation.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Threat actor demonstrates sophistication consistent with prior coordinated cases OR signature ties to a known threat actor or affiliated network.
response_protocols.legal_notes: Sharing surveillance signatures with law enforcement may carry information-sharing obligations or restrictions depending on jurisdiction and case context. Document the indicator constellation and observation conditions. This guidance does not constitute legal advice. Consult qualified legal counsel for jurisdiction-specific requirements.

tactics.field_notes: Surveillance Detection Countermeasures sort into three families: behavior obfuscation (varied routes, varied times, vehicle rotation, walk-then-drive transitions), persona obfuscation (cover stories, third-party proxies, fabricated employer affiliations to explain proximity to the target environment), and technical obfuscation (VPNs, Tor, burner phones, satellite or Street View imagery substituted for physical visits). The behavioral tell that separates a threat actor running SD-CMs from a careful private citizen is consistency — the threat actor varies the SAME behavior repeatedly in ways a private citizen would not, because the threat actor is solving for a specific surveillance-detection problem they expect the protected environment to have. An investigator catches SD-CM behavior by looking for over-engineered variance: too many vehicle changes for a single visit, too many short-distance walks before reaching the actual destination, too many cover stories that do not need to be cover stories. Detection of SD-CM behavior is itself a high-confidence indicator that the threat actor has reached operational sophistication and assumes a protective program is active around the targeted subject.
observed_contexts: executive protection case where the threat actor performed three vehicle changes within a four-mile corridor en route to repeated drive-bys of the targeted subject's residence
domestic case where the threat actor used a relative as a cutout to call the targeted subject's workplace and ask schedule-related questions, then later denied any such call had been made
insider-supported case where the threat actor relied entirely on satellite imagery and Street View for environmental survey to avoid generating any physical-observation signal
[literature: NTAC-MASS-2021 — pre-attack pattern of varied approaches and counter-surveillance behaviors observed in higher-sophistication mass attack cases]
extremist case where the threat actor used Tor and pseudonymous social media for all targeted-subject reconnaissance, with no clear-net signal until very late in the planning cycle

tactics.name: Operational Rehearsal
tactics.notes: Controlled dry run of the planned approach — timing assessments, route confirmation, access testing, go/no-go decision point validation. Operational rehearsal is a controlled exercise, not the live approach. Distinct from Partial Approach Rehearsal (TM0209), which uses the live target site with abort triggers.
tactics.cpn_notes: GPS and mapping apps, real-time traffic data, and satellite imagery are standard rehearsal planning tools. Digital simulation of timing and routing can substitute for physical rehearsal in some scenarios.

indicators.behavior: Threat actor performs repeated visits to the targeted subject's location at consistent times matching a planned attack window, without legitimate purpose
Threat actor drives or walks the planned approach route on multiple occasions, sometimes with stand-in vehicles or alternative timing to test variants
Threat actor times specific high-uncertainty operational segments — security shift change, building lockup, route arrival — repeatedly to validate planning assumptions
Threat actor conducts partial rehearsal of equipment or capability — weapon function checks at remote locations, vehicle handling tests, breach-tool practice — without revealing the operation
Threat actor uses stand-in targets — a comparable building or vehicle, a sim prop, or a role-player mimicking the individual — to rehearse execution without prematurely revealing intent
Threat actor's behavior at the targeted subject's environment shifts from observation to action-rehearsal — testing entry timing, identifying response gaps, walking the egress route

countermeasures.measure: Maintain behavioral-baseline awareness across the targeted subject's environment — coffee shops, parking facilities, perimeter — with reception and staff trained to flag repeat visitors who do not fit a recognizable pattern
countermeasures.limitations: Baseline awareness depends on stable staffing; high-turnover environments lose continuity. False positives are common where the protected environment overlaps with a high-foot-traffic neighborhood

countermeasures.measure: Implement multi-camera correlation across approach routes and adjacent locations to identify repeat presence consistent with rehearsal — same face, same vehicle, same behavioral pattern observed across non-adjacent points
countermeasures.limitations: Cross-camera correlation requires coverage density and analyst time or analytics support. Sophisticated threat actors rotate vehicles and clothing to defeat correlation

countermeasures.measure: Apply random-interval variation to security patterns — shift change times, lockup procedures, patrol routes — to defeat rehearsal-based timing capture
countermeasures.limitations: Operational predictability has legitimate value (staff coordination, contractor scheduling); over-randomization erodes effectiveness. Sophisticated threat actors infer the randomization schedule given enough observations

countermeasures.measure: Conduct after-action review of any unusual-behavior reports against the timeline of any subsequent attempted attack to identify retrospective rehearsal signals and refine baseline awareness training
countermeasures.limitations: Hindsight bias inflates the apparent clarity of pre-incident signals; retrospective patterns must be validated against negative cases to remain useful

response_protocols.trigger: Single Operational Rehearsal indicator detected (repeat presence at unusual times, route walk-through, equipment function check at the protected environment)
response_protocols.action: Document the indicator. Conduct a 5-business-day preliminary assessment that includes (a) corroboration through adjacent observations or camera review, (b) identification of any threat actor candidate, (c) cross-reference against open threat assessment cases. Determine whether the observed pattern is consistent with rehearsal or with legitimate routine.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Rehearsal pattern confirmed across multiple observations OR concurrent indicators surface from another Phase 1 or Phase 2 tactic.
response_protocols.legal_notes: Observation of an unidentified individual in public space generally requires no legal pre-clearance. Investigative escalation (identification, surveillance) carries jurisdiction-specific privacy implications. Document factually. This guidance does not constitute legal advice. Consult qualified legal counsel for jurisdiction-specific requirements.

response_protocols.trigger: Multiple Operational Rehearsal indicators co-observed for the same threat actor OR rehearsal coupled with confirmed capability acquisition, cover construction, or pathway indicators
response_protocols.action: Convene the threat management team within 24 hours. Conduct formal threat assessment. Implement enhanced protective posture for the targeted subject including route variation and surveillance detection. Coordinate with law enforcement; rehearsal-stage detection provides the strongest pre-incident interruption window. Initiate enhanced monitoring of the threat actor.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Rehearsal completion observed OR transition behavior toward execution stage.
response_protocols.legal_notes: Pre-incident interruption at rehearsal stage carries the highest preventive leverage; document the indicator constellation thoroughly to support any law enforcement engagement. Preserve evidence. This guidance does not constitute legal advice. Consult qualified legal counsel for jurisdiction-specific requirements.

tactics.field_notes: Operational Rehearsal is the threat actor's dress rehearsal — a partial or full walkthrough of the planned attack to test the plan against reality. It is often only recognizable in retrospect: the person sitting in the coffee shop across from the targeted subject's office didn't draw attention at the time; only after the attack does the cashier remember the man who came in three Tuesdays in a row, ordered the same drink, sat by the window, and left without finishing it. Most rehearsals are partial — the threat actor practices the breach but not the egress, or times the security shift but not the actual approach. Full rehearsals are rarer because they require operational artifacts (uniforms, weapons, vehicles) that themselves create detection signal. What an analyst is looking for is repeated presence at consistent times that no normal activity explains.
observed_contexts: executive protection case where the threat actor was identified after the attack as having visited the targeted subject's office building and adjacent coffee shop on multiple consecutive Tuesdays

workplace violence case where the threat actor performed weapon function checks at a remote rural site weeks before the attack, identified retrospectively through purchase records of range-style ammunition the threat actor had no documented sporting use for
domestic case where repeated drive-bys of the targeted subject's residence, varying time and direction across visits, were recognized as rehearsal only after the attack
[literature: NTAC-MASS-2021 — pre-attack rehearsal patterns documented in mass attacks against public spaces, including timing studies of security shift changes]
facility attack case where the threat actor performed partial rehearsal at a similar building (same architecture, same retail tenant) before targeting the actual location

tactics.name: Concealment
tactics.notes: Managing physical appearance and behavior to avoid detection under human observation. Actor blends into the environment appropriate to the location and context — adjusting dress, behavior, pace, and attention pattern to match expected profiles. Concealment is an ongoing behavioral discipline throughout the Approach phase, not a single action.

indicators.behavior: Threat actor's stated activity pattern develops gaps inconsistent with normal life — unaccounted-for time, unexplained absences, missing receipts or location data
Threat actor maintains compartmentalized communications — separate device, encrypted application, anonymous account — for operationally relevant contacts not used in normal life
Threat actor's online presence becomes selectively curated — deletion of grievance posts, suppression of identifiable statements of intent, removal of evidence from social media
Threat actor's financial pattern shows withdrawals or transfers consistent with cash or anonymized-payment operational expenses, with no corresponding documented purpose
Threat actor introduces inconsistencies between stated activities and physical or digital evidence — claimed locations not matching cell-tower data, claimed meetings with no corresponding records

Threat actor's behavior toward family members or peers becomes guarded — withdrawal from normal sharing, requests for privacy that exceed ordinary, irritability at routine questions about plans or whereabouts

countermeasures.measure: Maintain peer and family awareness of behavioral-change indicators — uncharacteristic withdrawal, evasiveness about plans, unexplained gaps in routine — with low-threshold reporting paths to security or threat assessment teams
countermeasures.limitations: Behavioral changes have many benign explanations (personal stress, depression, life events); reporting culture must encourage flagging without requiring certainty

countermeasures.measure: For organizationally-employed individuals already in the threat assessment caseload, monitor work-account patterns for compartmentalization signals — separate browser sessions, encrypted-tunnel activity, unusual access patterns
countermeasures.limitations: Encrypted tunnels and personal-device usage can defeat work-account monitoring. Privacy and labor-relations considerations require careful scoping

countermeasures.measure: Establish low-threshold reporting paths for associates who notice incongruity between another person's account of activities and observable evidence
countermeasures.limitations: Many incongruities have benign explanations and are not reported because the associate can't articulate why something feels off

countermeasures.measure: Conduct periodic financial-pattern analysis (where authorized) for individuals already in the active threat assessment caseload, focused on cash withdrawals, anonymized payments, and procurement consistent with operational expense profiles
countermeasures.limitations: Financial monitoring of identified individuals carries jurisdiction-specific legal constraints; cash transactions have many lawful uses

response_protocols.trigger: Single Concealment indicator reported (peer-report of behavioral change, financial pattern shift, online curation activity)
response_protocols.action: Document the indicator. Conduct a 5-business-day preliminary assessment that includes (a) corroboration through additional reports or data sources, (b) baseline review of the threat actor's prior behavioral pattern, (c) cross-reference against any active threat assessment case. Determine whether observed change rises to operational concern.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Concealment pattern coupled with concurrent indicators from another Phase 1 or Phase 2 tactic.
response_protocols.legal_notes: Behavioral observations of associates and family members are protected information; consult legal before any inquiry beyond the immediate report. Document factually. This guidance does not constitute legal advice. Consult qualified legal counsel for jurisdiction-specific requirements.

response_protocols.trigger: Multiple Concealment indicators co-observed for the same threat actor OR concealment activity coupled with capability acquisition, cover construction, or pathway-stage progression
response_protocols.action: Convene the threat management team within 24 hours. Conduct formal threat assessment. Concealment combined with other Phase 1/2 indicators is a high-confidence signal of operational sophistication and pending action. Implement enhanced protective posture. Coordinate with law enforcement.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Concealment pattern persists or intensifies OR pathway indicators progress through preparation stage.
response_protocols.legal_notes: Concealment is rarely unlawful in itself; the response posture is preventive intelligence, not criminal investigation, until concrete operational indicators surface. Document the indicator constellation thoroughly. This guidance does not constitute legal advice. Consult qualified legal counsel for jurisdiction-specific requirements.

tactics.field_notes: The signature of Concealment is what a security professional doesn't see — the meeting with no record, the trip with no documented purpose, the equipment that doesn't show up in any inventory. Concealment is constant through mobilization, and its only direct signal is when it fails. The threat actor reveals the operation through a slip, a contradiction, an artifact left where it shouldn't be — and that slip is often the only pre-execution signal a threat assessment team gets. The detection vector is the details that don't add up — a story that doesn't quite fit, a routine that doesn't quite match the cover, an absence where presence is expected. Concealment intensifies as the operation approaches execution; the threat actor is increasingly aware that any leak compromises the plan, and the discipline tightens accordingly.

domestic case where peer reports of evasiveness and unexplained nighttime absences preceded the attack by weeks, but were not aggregated to the threat assessment level until after the incident

extremist case where the threat actor curated their social media presence in the months before the attack — deleting older grievance posts and suppressing identifiable statements of intent — recognized as anti-forensic concealment in retrospect
[literature: FBI-PREATTACK-2018 — pre-attack pattern of financial withdrawals consistent with cash-based operational expense in active shooter cases]

insider threat case where compartmentalized communications via a separate device were detected through corroborating peer report and IT-anomaly observation, leading to interruption before mobilization completed

tactics.name: Perimeter Breach
tactics.notes: Defeating the outermost security layer protecting access to the subject — building perimeters, residential security, vehicle protection details, or controlled access zones. The method varies by target protective posture: social engineering for low-profile targets, technical defeat for hardened environments.
tactics.cpn_notes: Credential cloning, RFID/NFC skimming, and electronic lock exploit tools are cyber-enabled defeat methods that bypass physical barriers without direct force. Access control systems that are digitally exploitable change the threat calculus for protected subjects in secured environments.

indicators.behavior: Threat actor presents at a perimeter access point at off-hours or with timing inconsistent with verified visitor schedules, claimed appointments, or sponsoring contact
Threat actor attempts to bypass perimeter controls by tailgating an authorized individual through a secured access point
Threat actor uses a fabricated or stolen credential to attempt authorized passage through a perimeter access point
Threat actor defeats a physical perimeter control — climbing a fence, forcing a door, defeating an electronic lock — at a location not under active observation
Threat actor breaches the perimeter at a non-standard entry point — loading dock, service entrance, perimeter gap not under camera coverage
Threat actor's badge or credential is presented at the perimeter but the holder's biometric, photo, or behavioral profile does not match the credential's registered owner

countermeasures.measure: Maintain layered perimeter design with multiple sequential access controls so that a single-point breach does not yield interior access — outer fence, controlled entry, interior badge zones, sensitive-area additional barriers
countermeasures.limitations: Layered controls add cost and friction to legitimate operations. Insider sponsors with multi-tier access can defeat layering

countermeasures.measure: Conduct random-interval physical checks of non-primary perimeter access points — loading dock, service entrance, perimeter gaps — to validate posture and detect attempted breaches at unmanned locations
countermeasures.limitations: Random-interval checks have coverage gaps; sophisticated threat actors may infer the inspection cadence given enough observations

countermeasures.measure: Implement two-factor identity verification at perimeter access points — credential plus visual or biometric confirmation — for sensitivity-tiered locations
countermeasures.limitations: Two-factor friction can erode legitimate operations during high-traffic periods; biometric capture has privacy and regulatory implications

countermeasures.measure: Establish anti-tailgating training and physical controls — mantrap vestibule, single-occupant entry, badge re-validation — at high-sensitivity perimeter access points
countermeasures.limitations: Mantrap vestibules slow legitimate operations and may be bypassed via emergency exits or coordinated insider tailgating

response_protocols.trigger: Single Perimeter Breach indicator detected (off-hours unverified presence, tailgating attempt, fabricated credential at access point)
response_protocols.action: Detain the individual politely if lawful; verify identity through sponsoring contact or external corroboration. Notify the threat assessment team within the same business hour. Preserve any physical artifacts and access-attempt logs. Activate enhanced perimeter monitoring at adjacent access points.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Identity cannot be corroborated OR breach attempt connects to other concerning context (prior surveillance, prior cover construction).
response_protocols.legal_notes: Detention or extended challenge of an individual carries legal implications that vary by jurisdiction; coordinate with legal before any action beyond polite verification. Trespass and pretexting laws vary materially. This guidance does not constitute legal advice. Consult qualified legal counsel for jurisdiction-specific requirements.

response_protocols.trigger: Confirmed perimeter breach OR breach attempt coupled with capability acquisition or cover construction OR threat actor flees on challenge
response_protocols.action: Activate emergency response. Initiate facility lockdown per protocol. Notify law enforcement immediately. Implement enhanced protective posture for the targeted subject. Capture and preserve all physical and digital evidence of the breach attempt. Brief executive leadership.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Breach reaches sensitive interior area OR threat actor demonstrates means and proximity to the targeted subject.
response_protocols.legal_notes: Lockdown and emergency response are protective actions that do not require law enforcement authorization. Document the basis for initiating emergency protocols. Pretexting at protected sites and trespass into restricted areas may carry independent criminal liability; preserve evidence carefully. This guidance does not constitute legal advice. Consult qualified legal counsel for jurisdiction-specific requirements.

tactics.field_notes: Perimeter Breach almost never starts at the perimeter — by the time the threat actor reaches the breach point, the work was done in capability acquisition, cover construction, and rehearsal. The breach itself is often the easiest part of the operation because every choice that made it possible has already been made. Detection at the breach point is late detection by definition: every other tactic has failed to interrupt the threat actor. What surfaces in retrospect is usually the breach attempt that didn't quite fit — the contractor at the wrong gate, the badge that hadn't been swiped at expected interior checkpoints, the visitor whose sponsoring contact couldn't be reached. The most successful breaches in observed cases are the ones that didn't generate a detection signal until the threat actor was already inside the protected space.
observed_contexts: facility attack where the threat actor used a fabricated contractor uniform and prepared work-order documentation to pass perimeter reception, with the breach recognized only after cross-camera correlation in after-action review

executive protection case where a tailgating attempt at a parking-garage badge gate was caught by an alert security officer, leading to identification of the threat actor and interruption before reaching the targeted subject
insider-conspirator case where an external accomplice presented stolen credentials at a service entrance during a coordinated shift change, supported by an insider sponsor who validated the cover

Casework pattern: service-side access points — loading docks, vendor entrances, freight elevators — present a friendlier social-engineering surface than the front of house, and breach attempts during mobilization concentrate there

domestic attack at a protected residence where the threat actor breached the perimeter at a side gate with no camera coverage, with detection occurring only when the threat actor was already inside the property

tactics.name: Zone Penetration
tactics.notes: Moving through successive security layers after initial perimeter breach — from public space to controlled access, from controlled access to restricted zones, from restricted zones to the subject's location. Each layer requires a distinct access method; failure at any layer aborts the approach.
tactics.cpn_notes: Electronic lock bypass and elevator system manipulation extend the actor's reach through security-tiered environments. Physical security systems with digital control planes are vulnerable to zone penetration via cyber methods without physical force.

indicators.behavior: Threat actor's badge is swiped at an access point above the tier authorized for the credential holder, with the holder either physically present or credentials cloned
Threat actor moves through interior security tiers via tailgating, escort manipulation, or social engineering of personnel staffing each tier
Threat actor uses elevator system manipulation, electronic lock bypass, or door-control system manipulation to defeat tier-internal access controls without force
Threat actor's path through the protected environment matches a pre-determined route inconsistent with the destination claimed at perimeter or in visitor logs
Threat actor accesses interior security infrastructure (camera systems, alarm panels, communication systems) at any point during transit through tiered zones
Threat actor's interior access pattern shows pre-planning artifacts — knowledge of tier topology, badge zone boundaries, supervisory shift changes — inconsistent with a first-time visitor

countermeasures.measure: Implement zone-by-zone access logging with anomaly alerting for badge use at unfamiliar tiers, off-hours interior access, and access patterns inconsistent with the holder's job function
countermeasures.limitations: Anomaly tuning requires baseline behavioral data per credential holder; high-turnover environments produce excess false positives

countermeasures.measure: Maintain interior CCTV coverage at zone transitions with cross-camera correlation supporting retrospective path reconstruction across the entire protected environment
countermeasures.limitations: Coverage gaps and non-coverage zones (restrooms, executive offices) cannot be addressed by CCTV alone; cross-camera correlation requires either operator time or analytics support

countermeasures.measure: Deploy two-factor zone authentication at sensitive-tier transitions — badge plus visual identification, or badge plus biometric — with logging of authentication failures
countermeasures.limitations: Two-factor friction can erode legitimate operations during high-traffic periods; biometric capture has privacy and regulatory implications

countermeasures.measure: Establish escort accountability protocols requiring sponsoring contact identification, visit purpose validation, and continuous-presence requirements within sensitive tiers
countermeasures.limitations: Escort discipline degrades during sustained operations and across shift changes; staff with established relationships may relax verification under social pressure

response_protocols.trigger: Single Zone Penetration indicator detected (badge anomaly, cross-camera inconsistency, route mismatch with stated destination)
response_protocols.action: Document the indicator. Conduct same-business-day verification of the credential holder, the visit purpose, and the sponsoring contact. Pull cross-camera footage to reconstruct the threat actor's path. Notify the threat assessment team. Activate enhanced posture at adjacent sensitive tiers.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Verification fails OR path reconstruction reveals additional unauthorized tier access OR threat actor identity ties to prior threat case.
response_protocols.legal_notes: Interior CCTV footage and access logs are generally accessible under normal security policy; coordinate with legal before retention or sharing beyond standard policy. Document factually. This guidance does not constitute legal advice. Consult qualified legal counsel for jurisdiction-specific requirements.

response_protocols.trigger: Confirmed unauthorized zone penetration OR penetration coupled with capability acquisition, cover construction, or pathway-stage progression
response_protocols.action: Activate emergency response. Initiate facility lockdown or containment as appropriate to the tier breached. Notify law enforcement immediately. Implement enhanced protective posture for the targeted subject. Capture and preserve all physical and digital evidence including credentials, vehicles, and devices in the threat actor's possession.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Penetration reaches the targeted subject's immediate environment OR threat actor demonstrates means and proximity.
response_protocols.legal_notes: Trespass into restricted areas may carry independent criminal liability; preserve evidence carefully. Use of force by security personnel is governed by jurisdiction-specific authority. This guidance does not constitute legal advice. Consult qualified legal counsel for jurisdiction-specific requirements.

tactics.field_notes: The signature of Zone Penetration is movement through a building that doesn't match the threat actor's stated reason for being there — a contractor on an executive floor, a vendor in a restricted communications room, a visitor escorted past the meeting room and never seen exiting. Each tier of a layered security design exists because the previous tier admitted someone whose access at the next tier wasn't validated. What an investigator looks for is the badge swipe at a tier above the holder's authorization, the appearance in CCTV at a location the threat actor has no apparent business being, and the timing pattern that suggests the path was rehearsed. Zone Penetration tactics range from low-tech (tailgating one tier, then social-engineering the next) to high-tech (cloning credentials at one tier and using elevator-system manipulation to reach another). The detection difficulty rises with each tier: by the time the threat actor reaches the targeted subject's immediate environment, the upstream tiers have already failed.
observed_contexts: executive protection case where a contractor with valid lobby-tier access tailgated through three interior tiers via successive social engineering of staff at each transition, identified retrospectively through cross-camera correlation
facility attack where the threat actor cloned a maintenance-tier badge and used elevator-system manipulation to reach an executive floor without ever interacting with reception or escort staff

insider-conspirator case where an external accomplice was escorted by an insider sponsor through multiple zones with no zone-by-zone verification, allowing access to a sensitive area outside the sponsor's authorization

Across casework, tailgating and escort manipulation are the standard methods for moving across interior access tiers — attaching to legitimate movement rather than presenting credentials, especially at the edges between public-facing and restricted zones

domestic attack at a protected residence where the threat actor entered via the perimeter then defeated three interior locks in sequence using bump-key tools, recognized through audio sensor logs in retrospect

tactics.name: Access Elevation
tactics.notes: Gaining higher-tier physical access through deception, social engineering, or credential abuse rather than force. Actor obtains access rights or physical proximity that their actual status does not authorize — vendor badge, escort manipulation, insider assistance. Distinct from Barrier Defeat (TM0302), which uses force.
tactics.cpn_notes: Cloned access credentials, spoofed caller ID, and fabricated digital authorization documents enable access elevation without physical contact. Attackers may use digitally-generated fake work orders or appointment confirmations to pass social engineering checkpoints.

indicators.behavior: Threat actor presents a fabricated or borrowed credential to a guard, receptionist, or escort to gain access above the tier their actual status authorizes

Threat actor exploits an authorized escort relationship to access a tier the threat actor cannot enter independently — vendor escorted into an executive area, contractor accompanied to a restricted server room
Threat actor uses social engineering — pretexted phone calls, urgent-need framing, name-dropping a senior — to convince personnel to grant access not normally extended
Threat actor's claimed sponsoring contact does not exist, is uncontactable, or denies the engagement when verified
Threat actor uses a cloned access credential, fabricated work order, or spoofed appointment confirmation to pass automated or human verification at an access point
Threat actor's access elevation creates an audit anomaly — a badge holder appearing at a tier inconsistent with role, a visitor with no sponsoring record, a contractor with no work-order match

countermeasures.measure: Require sponsoring-contact callback verification for all visitor access at sensitive tiers, with no admission until the sponsoring contact independently confirms the engagement
countermeasures.limitations: Callback verification slows legitimate operations and is often relaxed by reception staff under pressure to admit waiting visitors

countermeasures.measure: Implement work-order matching protocols requiring vendor and contractor visits to align with a pre-recorded order in the maintenance system before access is granted
countermeasures.limitations: Requires disciplined work-order entry that contractors may bypass for emergency calls; maintenance system integration adds operational overhead

countermeasures.measure: Train reception, escort personnel, and sensitive-tier custodians on common social-engineering pretexts including urgent-need framing, senior-name-dropping, and credential-loss claims
countermeasures.limitations: Training fades; staff turnover requires constant refresh. Effectiveness depends on a culture that empowers personnel to challenge senior-appearing requests

countermeasures.measure: Deploy biometric or multi-factor verification at sensitive-tier access points to defeat cloned or borrowed credentials
countermeasures.limitations: Biometric capture has privacy and regulatory implications; cost and friction may be unjustified for lower-sensitivity tiers

response_protocols.trigger: Single Access Elevation indicator detected (sponsoring contact unverifiable, badge tier mismatch, suspected social-engineering attempt)
response_protocols.action: Detain the individual politely if on-site; verify identity through independent channels including direct contact with the named sponsoring person. Notify the threat assessment team within the same business hour. Preserve any physical artifacts including credentials, work orders, and business cards. Pull access logs for review.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Identity cannot be verified OR access elevation connects to other concerning context (prior surveillance, prior cover construction, prior attempted approach).
response_protocols.legal_notes: Detention or extended challenge of an individual carries legal implications; coordinate with legal before any action beyond polite verification. Pretexting at protected sites may itself be unlawful in some jurisdictions. This guidance does not constitute legal advice. Consult qualified legal counsel for jurisdiction-specific requirements.

response_protocols.trigger: Confirmed access elevation past sensitive-tier controls OR access elevation coupled with capability acquisition or rehearsal indicators
response_protocols.action: Activate emergency response. Initiate sensitive-tier lockdown. Notify law enforcement. Implement enhanced protective posture for the targeted subject. Capture all physical and digital evidence including the threat actor's credentials and the audit trail of the elevation pathway. Brief executive leadership.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Threat actor reaches the targeted subject's tier OR demonstrates means and proximity.
response_protocols.legal_notes: Pretexting and unauthorized access at protected sites may carry independent criminal liability; preserve evidence under chain-of-custody discipline. This guidance does not constitute legal advice. Consult qualified legal counsel for jurisdiction-specific requirements.

tactics.field_notes: Access Elevation is the threat actor's exploitation of trust — gaining higher-tier physical access through deception, social engineering, or credential abuse rather than force. There's no physical signal in Access Elevation: no broken lock, no climbed fence, no tackled guard. The detection signal is the audit trail: the badge swipe at the wrong tier, the visitor log with a name nobody can verify, the contractor with no matching work order. Access Elevation is constant work for the threat actor because every successful elevation expires when the access window closes; the threat actor is not just gaining access once but maintaining the cover that justifies returning. An investigator catches Access Elevation by treating the audit trail as the primary evidence and validating each elevation against the holder's actual authorization.
observed_contexts: executive protection case where a threat actor presented a stolen contractor badge at reception, was escorted to a senior executive's floor, and was identified only when the escort attempted callback verification post-meeting

domestic protection case where a threat actor used a pretexted urgent-need claim — claiming to be a family member's friend with a delivery — to gain residence access, identified retrospectively through doorbell camera recovery
insider-conspirator case where the threat actor's elevation was sponsored by an insider, with the audit trail showing a series of badge swipes at tiers inconsistent with the contractor role on file

Casework pattern: access elevation through cover-for-action — the threat actor presents in a role that grants higher access than their actual status authorizes — vendor, contractor, visiting executive, IT support, or a social-engineering call to reception that produces a temporary badge — and operates from inside that elevated tier without the friction of credential challenges
facility attack case where the threat actor used a cloned employee badge to bypass automated verification, with the elevation recognized only after post-incident audit-trail analysis

tactics.name: Position Establishment
tactics.notes: Achieving and holding the physical position required to execute the planned action against the subject. Position establishment may be brief (a sniper position held for minutes) or sustained (a surveillance position maintained over days). The position is the final precondition before Phase 3 can begin.

indicators.behavior: Threat actor is observed in a static position at a location offering line-of-sight, approach angle, or proximity to the targeted subject's anticipated arrival, departure, or routine location
Threat actor has positioned a vehicle, equipment, or staging materials at the position consistent with sustained occupation rather than transient presence

Threat actor's position is held over a duration inconsistent with normal routine activity at that location — a person at a coffee shop window for three hours, a vehicle in a parking spot with no occupants for an extended period
Threat actor's position is selected for line-of-sight to a known route, residence, vehicle, or appointment of the targeted subject, with the position itself offering concealment or visual cover
Threat actor's position behavior shows operational alertness — repeated horizon scanning, watch-checking, repeated phone glances, or device-monitoring behavior — inconsistent with passive presence

countermeasures.measure: Conduct surveillance detection sweeps of known approach corridors and vantage points at consistent intervals, particularly during the targeted subject's routine arrival, departure, and known appointment windows
countermeasures.limitations: Sweep schedules may themselves become observable to the threat actor; trained operators are required to distinguish operational alertness from routine waiting

countermeasures.measure: Deploy CCTV coverage of approach angles and likely vantage points associated with the protected environment, with automated alerting for sustained presence beyond a threshold duration
countermeasures.limitations: Sustained-presence thresholds must balance false positives against missing brief positions; coverage gaps in adjacent public space limit effectiveness

countermeasures.measure: Train reception, lobby personnel, parking attendants, and adjacent business staff (coffee shops, retail tenants) on indicators of operationally-alert presence inconsistent with patron behavior
countermeasures.limitations: Awareness fades without reinforcement; adjacent business cooperation requires established relationships and may be subject to staff turnover

countermeasures.measure: Vary the targeted subject's routine timing and route across observable schedule periods to deny the threat actor a stable position-establishment opportunity
countermeasures.limitations: Route variation has operational and personal cost for the targeted subject; sophisticated threat actors infer the variation pattern given enough observations

response_protocols.trigger: Single Position Establishment indicator detected (sustained presence at a vantage point, staged vehicle with no occupant, operationally-alert behavior at proximity to the targeted subject's routine)
response_protocols.action: Document the indicator. Conduct same-business-day verification through additional observation, CCTV review, and cross-camera correlation. Notify the threat assessment team. Activate enhanced surveillance detection at adjacent vantage points. Brief the targeted subject on observed indicator and consider route variation.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Sustained presence confirmed across multiple observations OR position is selected for line-of-sight to the targeted subject's routine.
response_protocols.legal_notes: Observation of an unidentified person in public space generally requires no legal pre-clearance. Investigative escalation carries jurisdiction-specific privacy implications. Document factually. This guidance does not constitute legal advice. Consult qualified legal counsel for jurisdiction-specific requirements.

response_protocols.trigger: Confirmed Position Establishment with operational alertness OR position coupled with capability acquisition, rehearsal, or pathway-stage progression
response_protocols.action: Convene the threat management team within 24 hours. Conduct full risk assessment. Implement enhanced protective posture including immediate route variation and on-site response capability deployment. Coordinate with law enforcement; sustained position with apparent operational intent is a high-confidence pre-execution signal.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Threat actor identified with means and demonstrates intent to act OR transitions from position to approach.
response_protocols.legal_notes: Pre-execution interruption at Position Establishment carries the highest preventive leverage in the late mobilization window. Document the indicator constellation thoroughly. This guidance does not constitute legal advice. Consult qualified legal counsel for jurisdiction-specific requirements.

tactics.field_notes: Position Establishment is the final precondition before execution — the threat actor has reached the location, achieved the angle, the proximity, the line-of-sight, and now waits for the final commitment trigger. Everything before this point was movement; everything after is action. The position can be brief (a sniper position held for minutes) or sustained (a surveillance position maintained over days), and the duration shapes detection: brief positions leave little signal, sustained positions create the encounter window where presence becomes observable. The threat actor at this stage is increasingly committed and decreasingly mobile. What an analyst is looking for is the person who has stopped, who has chosen a vantage point, and whose proximity to the targeted subject's environment cannot be explained by routine.
observed_contexts: executive protection case where the threat actor occupied a coffee shop window seat across from the targeted subject's office for three consecutive mornings, identified by the cashier through baseline-awareness training
domestic case where the threat actor staged a vehicle at a vantage point overlooking the targeted subject's residence for multiple nights, recognized through cross-camera correlation in retrospect
active shooter event where the threat actor held a position in a parking garage stairwell with line-of-sight to the building entrance for nearly forty minutes before the kinetic moment
[literature: NTAC-MASS-2021 — pre-attack pattern of static-position observation prior to mass attacks against public spaces]

facility attack where the threat actor's operational alertness behaviors (horizon scanning, watch-checking) were captured on CCTV but not aggregated to a threat assessment trigger until after-action review

tactics.name: Operational Pause
tactics.notes: Deliberate stand-down to allow counter-surveillance conditions to clear, security posture to relax, an environmental opportunity to materialize, or to adapt to changes such as shifts in resource availability or information gathered during Target Development becoming no longer viable. Operational pause is a risk management decision — the actor may choose to wait due to internal or external factors that may not surface until later. Generates cold trails that complicate later investigation.

indicators.behavior: Threat actor maintains observable presence near the targeted subject's environment over multiple days or weeks without apparent purpose and without proceeding to action

Threat actor's presence pattern shows return-after-withdrawal behavior — leaving the area, then returning at a later time matching changed conditions (different shift, different day-of-week, different security posture)
Threat actor maintains operational artifacts (vehicle staged, equipment cached, cover identity active) over a duration that suggests sustained pause rather than abandonment

Threat actor's communications, financial activity, or online behavior shows continued operational tempo — research on the targeted subject, operationally-relevant procurement — inconsistent with a routine waiting period

Threat actor's pause coincides with observable environmental triggers — increased security posture, public attention to the targeted subject, news of an unrelated similar attack — indicating tactical patience rather than abandonment

countermeasures.measure: Maintain elevated surveillance detection posture for an extended period after any concerning indicator surfaces; the threat actor's response to detection may be pause rather than abandonment
countermeasures.limitations: Sustained elevated posture has high resource cost; threat assessment teams cannot maintain peak alertness indefinitely without burnout

countermeasures.measure: Track cases through the threat assessment caseload over time rather than closing them prematurely on absence of activity; Operational Pause is one of the most common reasons a case appears to close and then re-emerges
countermeasures.limitations: Caseload size constraints force closure decisions; analyst attention is finite and case re-emergence may not be recognized as the same threat actor without caseload-management discipline

countermeasures.measure: Implement variable security posture across observable schedule periods to deny the threat actor a stable assessment of conditions to wait out
countermeasures.limitations: Variation has operational cost and may itself become observable to a sustained-pause threat actor given enough observations

countermeasures.measure: Conduct periodic re-assessment of cases in pause status, particularly at known trigger windows including anniversary dates, public events involving the targeted subject, and concurrent crisis periods
countermeasures.limitations: Trigger windows are inferred and may not align with the threat actor's actual decision points; re-assessment overhead must be balanced against active-case workload

response_protocols.trigger: Threat actor in established pause status (case open, indicators previously surfaced, no kinetic activity) shows behavioral change consistent with end of pause — return to environment, resumed operational tempo, environmental trigger event
response_protocols.action: Reactivate the case to active monitoring. Brief the threat assessment team on the trigger event. Conduct rapid baseline review of the threat actor's recent communications, movement, and procurement. Implement enhanced protective posture for the targeted subject. Consider pre-emptive coordination with law enforcement.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Pause-end behavior progresses to position establishment, capability acquisition resumption, or pathway-stage advancement.
response_protocols.legal_notes: Reactivation of dormant cases must follow caseload-management policy; document the trigger event and behavioral basis for the reactivation decision. This guidance does not constitute legal advice. Consult qualified legal counsel for jurisdiction-specific requirements.

response_protocols.trigger: Pause ends with confirmed return to operational tempo coupled with capability acquisition, rehearsal, or position establishment at the targeted subject's environment
response_protocols.action: Convene the threat management team within 24 hours. Conduct formal threat assessment. Implement enhanced protective posture. Coordinate with law enforcement; pause-end transitions are a high-confidence pre-execution signal because the threat actor is moving from waiting to action.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Threat actor demonstrates means and proximity to the targeted subject after pause ends.
response_protocols.legal_notes: Pause-end activity may not by itself constitute criminal conduct; the response posture is preventive intelligence until concrete operational indicators surface. Document the indicator constellation thoroughly. This guidance does not constitute legal advice. Consult qualified legal counsel for jurisdiction-specific requirements.

tactics.field_notes: Operational Pause is the tactic that looks like nothing happening — the threat actor has reached position, has the means, and is choosing to wait. The pause is a risk-management decision, not a failure to act: counter-surveillance heat, security posture, environmental conditions, or absence of the targeted subject have produced an unfavorable window, and the threat actor would rather wait for a better one than commit to a degraded operation.
