Each leads to a different withdrawal posture: a successful withdrawal is rapid and pre-planned; a failed withdrawal is improvised and often visible to bystanders; an aborted withdrawal looks like routine departure with no incident at all. Some threat actors don't plan withdrawal — the operational plan ends at execution, with the threat actor expecting to be captured, killed, or to take their own life. The presence or absence of a withdrawal plan is itself diagnostic of actor type: organized criminal threat actors plan withdrawal carefully; ideologically-driven threat actors often don't. Detection during withdrawal depends on rapid coordination between security personnel, law enforcement, and CCTV operators — the threat actor is moving through public space at speed, and the detection window is narrower than at any other stage of the operation.
observed_contexts: active shooter event with planned withdrawal where the threat actor changed vehicles at a pre-staged location two miles from the scene, escaping initial perimeter establishment by approximately fifteen minutes
ideologically-driven attack where the threat actor made no withdrawal attempt, surrendering at the scene as part of a planned attribution claim
workplace violence event with improvised withdrawal where the threat actor's panic-driven route through a public area was captured on multiple CCTV systems, supporting rapid identification
[literature: NTAC-MASS-2021 — pattern of withdrawal planning differences between organized and ideologically-driven threat actors at mass attacks against public spaces]

domestic attack at a residence where the threat actor's withdrawal route deliberately avoided arterial roads and known camera positions, identified retrospectively through cross-jurisdictional CCTV correlation

tactics.name: Evidence Management
tactics.notes: Counter-forensics actions to reduce the traceability of the operation — physical evidence destruction, digital cleanup, biological material management, scene staging. The sophistication of evidence management is a reliable actor classification signal: lone actors rarely execute systematic counter-forensics; state actors plan it as a Phase 1 requirement.

indicators.behavior: Threat actor wipes or destroys electronic devices — phones, computers, storage media — before, during, or after the operation
Threat actor disposes of operationally relevant clothing, weapons, vehicles, or equipment in locations or via methods designed to prevent recovery
Threat actor relocates artifacts — manifestos, planning materials, documentation — from operationally relevant locations (residence, vehicle) to dead-drop or third-party storage
Threat actor stages artifacts at the scene or related locations to misdirect investigation toward an unrelated party, motive, or method
Threat actor maintains operational discipline that prevents accumulation of evidence in the first place — minimal communications, cash transactions, no documentation of planning steps
Threat actor's online presence is reduced or curated post-incident — account deletion, content removal, identity scrubbing — consistent with anti-forensic post-action behavior

countermeasures.measure: Maintain rapid scene-control protocols at the protected environment, including chain-of-custody discipline for any artifact recovered before law enforcement arrival
countermeasures.limitations: Scene control depends on trained personnel and may be impractical during ongoing kinetic activity. Chain-of-custody integrity is fragile and easily compromised under stress

countermeasures.measure: Coordinate with law enforcement on digital-forensic readiness — pre-established procedures for device imaging, network log preservation, and evidence handling consistent with admissibility requirements
countermeasures.limitations: Digital forensic readiness requires specialized expertise that may not be available in-house; jurisdictional admissibility standards vary

countermeasures.measure: Implement post-incident social media and communications monitoring of identified threat actors and known associates for evidence-management behavior including account deletion, content removal, and timeline curation
countermeasures.limitations: Monitoring of post-incident behavior carries legal scope and authorization constraints; closed platforms are not visible without legal process

countermeasures.measure: Maintain forensic-awareness training for security personnel and reception staff covering common evidence-management patterns and the diagnostic value of absent expected artifacts at the scene
countermeasures.limitations: Awareness training cannot substitute for trained forensic personnel during actual incident response. Detection of evidence-absence requires baseline knowledge of what should be present

response_protocols.trigger: Evidence management indicators detected post-incident at the protected environment, at the threat actor's residence, or in associated digital infrastructure
response_protocols.action: Activate scene-control and chain-of-custody discipline. Coordinate with law enforcement on forensic recovery. Initiate post-incident monitoring of the threat actor's online presence and associate communications. Document any artifact absence relative to expected baseline. Brief the threat assessment team on evidence-management patterns observed.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Evidence management discipline indicates organized threat actor or expanded network requiring broader investigation.
response_protocols.legal_notes: Chain-of-custody integrity is critical for any subsequent prosecution. Post-incident monitoring of the threat actor and associates carries jurisdiction-specific authorization requirements. This guidance does not constitute legal advice. Consult qualified legal counsel for jurisdiction-specific requirements.

response_protocols.trigger: Sustained anti-forensic discipline detected during ongoing investigation suggesting organized operational sophistication or network involvement
response_protocols.action: Coordinate with law enforcement on expanded forensic-recovery effort including dead-drop searches, third-party storage facility records, and associate-residence searches under appropriate legal process. Treat the anti-forensic pattern as diagnostic input to the threat actor profile and adjust investigative posture accordingly.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Anti-forensic pattern reveals connection to known organized threat group or expanded operational network.
response_protocols.legal_notes: Expanded searches under legal process require probable cause supported by documented evidence-management indicators. Coordinate with prosecutors before any covert action. This guidance does not constitute legal advice. Consult qualified legal counsel for jurisdiction-specific requirements.

tactics.field_notes: Evidence Management sorts into three approaches: destruction (devices wiped, weapons disposed of, clothing burned), concealment (artifacts moved to a location not associated with the threat actor), and staging (artifacts deliberately placed to misdirect investigation). The approach a threat actor chooses depends on time available after the operation, the resources at hand, and whether the threat actor expects to be identified at all. In observed cases, evidence-management discipline is one of the strongest predictors of operational sophistication: an organized threat actor maintains anti-forensic practice from planning through aftermath; an ideologically-driven threat actor often makes no attempt to manage evidence and may deliberately preserve artifacts as part of an attribution claim. Detection during evidence management depends on rapid scene control, forensic literacy, and coordination with law enforcement — each recovered artifact or fragment shifts the investigative balance, and threat-actor counter-forensic effort is itself observable through the absence of expected artifacts at the scene.
observed_contexts: active shooter event where the threat actor's mobile device was destroyed at the scene (battery removed, screen smashed, storage drilled), recognized as planned anti-forensic behavior in after-action review
ideologically-driven attack where the threat actor preserved a manifesto and uploaded it to multiple platforms before the kinetic phase, prioritizing attribution over anti-forensic discipline

workplace violence case where the threat actor's residence search recovered an absence of expected artifacts (no laptop, no recent purchase records, no journals) consistent with pre-incident relocation of operational evidence
[literature: FBI-PREATTACK-2018 — pattern of pre-attack anti-forensic discipline at a subset of active shooter cases including device wiping and timeline curation]
insider conspirator case where post-incident social media curation by a known associate revealed the network's operational discipline and supported expanded investigation

tactics.name: Cover Reestablishment
tactics.notes: Returning to a normal behavioral envelope after the operation — reestablishing the appearance that the actor was not involved. Includes alibi establishment, contact normalization with colleagues and associates, and behavioral management to avoid post-incident detection.

indicators.behavior: Threat actor establishes a documented alibi for the operational window — credit card use at distant location, confirmed social media activity, witnessed presence at a venue inconsistent with operational location

Threat actor's contact pattern with colleagues, family, and associates resumes at a cadence and tone matching pre-operation baseline, without deviation that would suggest psychological residue from the operation
Threat actor returns to normal routine activities — workplace attendance, hobbies, social engagements — within a timeframe consistent with pre-operation behavior
Threat actor's online presence shows deliberate normalization — routine posts, no commemoration of the operation, no behavioral break that would draw attention
Threat actor's response to the operation in conversation matches the response of an uninvolved peer — appropriate concern, no insider knowledge that wasn't publicly available

countermeasures.measure: Maintain peer and family awareness of post-incident behavioral baseline indicators including over-rehearsed alibis, atypical reluctance to discuss the incident, or inconsistencies between claimed and verifiable activities
countermeasures.limitations: Many associates of a successful threat actor are themselves disinclined to suspect; reporting threshold is high in close personal relationships

countermeasures.measure: Coordinate with law enforcement on cross-reference of alibi claims against transaction records, location data, and witness reports for high-confidence threat actor candidates
countermeasures.limitations: Cross-reference depends on retained records that may be unavailable across jurisdictions or platforms; alibi claims that are partially true are harder to invalidate than fully fabricated ones

countermeasures.measure: Conduct extended monitoring of high-confidence threat actor candidates beyond the immediate post-incident window — Cover Reestablishment is most observable when the threat actor's discipline begins to slip, which can occur on widely varying timelines depending on the actor and operational pressure
countermeasures.limitations: Extended monitoring requires sustained analyst attention and legal scope; without a high-confidence candidate, monitoring is unfocused and produces noise rather than detection

countermeasures.measure: Establish information-sharing with law enforcement on behavioral patterns characteristic of post-incident cover reestablishment, including over-rehearsed alibi structures and contact-pattern normalization signatures
countermeasures.limitations: Pattern documentation lags adversary behavior; signatures characteristic of one threat actor class may not generalize to others

response_protocols.trigger: Single Cover Reestablishment indicator detected for a threat actor candidate (alibi inconsistency, behavioral baseline anomaly, online normalization signal)
response_protocols.action: Document the indicator. Coordinate with law enforcement on cross-reference of the alibi claim against available records. Conduct baseline review of the threat actor candidate's pre-operation activity pattern. Notify the threat assessment team for inclusion in any active case.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Multiple indicators tied to the same threat actor candidate OR alibi cross-reference fails OR behavioral pattern reveals operationally-relevant inconsistency.
response_protocols.legal_notes: Investigation of an individual's behavioral pattern and alibi claim carries jurisdiction-specific privacy implications; coordinate with legal before any escalation. This guidance does not constitute legal advice. Consult qualified legal counsel for jurisdiction-specific requirements.

response_protocols.trigger: Multiple Cover Reestablishment indicators tied to a high-confidence threat actor candidate, particularly where indicators surface across the one-to-three-month post-event window
response_protocols.action: Coordinate with law enforcement on enhanced post-incident investigation. Apply forensic discipline to alibi cross-reference, behavioral pattern reconstruction, and online-presence analysis. Brief the threat assessment team and executive leadership on the candidate's standing in active investigation.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Cover Reestablishment evidence supports formal investigation OR ties to other open threat cases.
response_protocols.legal_notes: Sustained investigation of an individual requires evidentiary support; coordinate with prosecutors on the threshold for formal action. This guidance does not constitute legal advice. Consult qualified legal counsel for jurisdiction-specific requirements.

tactics.field_notes: Cover Reestablishment is the inverse of Cover Construction. Where Cover Construction builds a fabricated identity to enable approach, Cover Reestablishment restores the threat actor's pre-operation identity to deflect attribution. The threat actor at this stage is performing absence: appearing at expected places at expected times, resuming routine social and professional contacts, generating no behavioral signal that would distinguish them from someone who had not just executed an operation. The question for the threat assessment team is whether the threat actor's behavioral envelope has reverted to something indistinguishable from normal — and what surfaces during the tactic is behavioral signals that don't quite fit: the routine that's slightly off, the contact pattern that's resumed too quickly or too slowly, the alibi that holds at first inspection but doesn't survive cross-reference.
observed_contexts: workplace violence case where the threat actor returned to work the day after the attack and conducted routine duties with no apparent change in pattern, identified retrospectively when alibi cross-reference revealed a 90-minute gap unaccounted for during the operational window

domestic case where the threat actor's contact pattern with extended family resumed within 48 hours of the incident, recognized as deliberate cover behavior only when peer reports of over-rehearsed alibi answers aggregated across multiple interviews

executive protection case where the threat actor's online presence showed a deliberate gap in posting during the operational window followed by a normalized pattern, identified through retrospective social-media archival analysis

[literature: FBI-PREATTACK-2018 — pattern of post-incident behavioral normalization in active shooter cases, with disciplined return to routine identified as a marker of pre-meditation rather than impulsive attack]

insider threat case where the threat actor's resumed workplace routine showed the precise tone-matching of pre-incident peer interactions but failed under cross-reference of badge-swipe patterns inconsistent with claimed activities

tactics.name: Network Protection
tactics.notes: Protecting remaining members of the operational network — communication shutdown, personnel dispersal, infrastructure removal, and cutout management. For organized actors, network protection determines whether a single operation exposure becomes a network-wide compromise. For lone actors, this tactic is absent.

indicators.behavior: Threat actor initiates communications shutdown across the operational network — devices destroyed, accounts deleted, channels abandoned, encrypted-app contact lists wiped
Threat actor disperses operational personnel away from the protected environment, the targeted subject's region, or any location associated with the operation
Threat actor removes operational infrastructure including safe houses, vehicle staging, equipment caches, and digital infrastructure used during the operation
Threat actor manages witting accomplices through payment, reassignment, relocation, or in extreme cases threatened or actual harm to ensure silence under post-incident questioning

Threat actor manages unwitting cutouts (proxy purchasers, transportation providers, document forgers) through compartmentalization, payment, or removal of operational connection — the cutout often not knowing they were operationally relevant
Threat actor's network response to law enforcement contact with any single accomplice shows pre-coordinated discipline — silence, lawyer-up, denial, or pre-arranged story

countermeasures.measure: Coordinate with law enforcement on rapid post-incident interview and forensic recovery across identified accomplice nodes before network protection completes — the post-incident window is bounded and shrinking
countermeasures.limitations: Rapid interview depends on accomplice identification within the post-incident window; sophisticated networks pre-coordinate dispersal that places accomplices outside reach

countermeasures.measure: Maintain capability to track accomplice movement, communication, and financial activity in the post-incident window through coordinated law enforcement and intelligence-sharing channels
countermeasures.limitations: Tracking carries jurisdiction-specific authorization requirements; cross-border movement requires international coordination that may lag the threat actor's dispersal speed

countermeasures.measure: Establish legal-process pathways for compelling accomplice testimony where evidence supports it, including immunity offers and witness protection where appropriate
countermeasures.limitations: Compelled testimony depends on prosecutor judgment and witness reliability; pre-coordinated network discipline may resist immunity offers when leadership is at risk

countermeasures.measure: Implement coordination with international counterparts where network protection involves cross-border movement of accomplices or assets, particularly into jurisdictions with limited extradition or cooperation
countermeasures.limitations: International coordination is constrained by treaty, diplomatic relations, and political considerations that may not align with operational urgency

response_protocols.trigger: Network protection indicators detected post-incident — communications shutdown across multiple nodes, personnel dispersal, infrastructure removal, accomplice management activity
response_protocols.action: Activate rapid post-incident investigation. Coordinate with law enforcement on accomplice identification, interview deployment, and forensic recovery. Treat the post-incident window as the primary detection opportunity; once network protection completes, attribution becomes materially harder.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Network protection signature ties to known organized adversary OR cross-border movement initiated.
response_protocols.legal_notes: Investigation of multi-actor networks requires coordination across jurisdictional and prosecutorial authority; chain-of-custody integrity for any artifact recovered is critical for downstream prosecution. This guidance does not constitute legal advice. Consult qualified legal counsel for jurisdiction-specific requirements.

response_protocols.trigger: Sustained network-protection discipline detected during ongoing investigation indicating organized operational sophistication and broader network involvement
response_protocols.action: Treat the network-protection pattern as diagnostic input to threat actor profile and adjust investigative posture accordingly. Coordinate with intelligence-sharing partners on signature recognition. Document the network's discipline pattern for inclusion in adversary tradecraft database. Consider expanded legal process where evidentiary support permits.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Network-protection pattern reveals connection to known organized threat group or expanded operational network.
response_protocols.legal_notes: Expanded legal process requires evidentiary threshold; coordinate with prosecutors before any covert investigative step. Information-sharing with intelligence partners may carry classification or jurisdictional restrictions. This guidance does not constitute legal advice. Consult qualified legal counsel for jurisdiction-specific requirements.

tactics.field_notes: Network Protection effectiveness depends on operational discipline and compartmentation across the entire operational network. If every member maintained strict OPSEC, the loss of one accomplice exposes only what that accomplice knew — often a single operational role rather than the broader operation. If a segment of the network practiced poor OPSEC, exposure of any member in that segment may compromise the entire segment, while well-disciplined compartments remain protected behind the operational firewall. The threat actor leading the operation is responsible at this stage for shutting down communications, dispersing personnel, removing infrastructure, and managing cutouts before any single accomplice is interviewed by law enforcement. For lone-actor operations this tactic is absent, which is itself diagnostic. For organized actors, Network Protection determines whether the operation generates one prosecution, one segment exposed, or many.
observed_contexts: kidnapping case where the threat actor's network protection succeeded for two of three accomplices (devices wiped, dispersal completed, payments made) but the third accomplice's failure to wipe a single device produced the forensic seam that identified the network

extremist case where pre-coordinated network discipline (silence, lawyer-up, pre-arranged story) held across initial interviews but unraveled after immunity offers were extended to mid-tier accomplices over a six-month investigation

transnational organized case where rapid cross-border dispersal placed the operational lead and senior accomplices outside extradition before post-incident interviews could be conducted, with the case resolving only against domestic-tier accomplices
[literature: NITTF-GUIDE-2017 — pattern of insider-network discipline post-incident, including pre-coordinated response protocols and the diagnostic value of network-protection sophistication]
lone-actor case where the absence of any network-protection signature was correctly read as confirmation of lone-actor profile, simplifying the post-incident investigation focus

tactics.name: Financial Disposition
tactics.notes: Processing ransom payments, receiving contracted payment for professional actors, moving funds to obscure origin, and managing cryptocurrency associated with the operation. Financial Disposition is present when a financial motive exists — kidnap-for-ransom, contract operations, extortion.
tactics.cpn_notes: Cryptocurrency is the primary post-operation payment mechanism for both ransom and contract operations. Mixing services, chain hopping, and privacy coins are the standard obfuscation chain. Financial forensics on blockchain transactions have become a primary investigative tool — sophistication of financial disposition directly determines investigative success.

indicators.behavior: Threat actor receives ransom payment, contract payment, or extortion proceeds via cryptocurrency, prepaid cards, wire transfer, or hawala consistent with the operation's financial scale

Threat actor uses cryptocurrency mixing services, chain hopping across multiple wallets, privacy coins (Monero, Zcash), or DeFi protocols to obfuscate the link between operational receipt and the threat actor's accessible wallet

Threat actor converts operational proceeds into legitimate-appearing forms — real estate purchases, business investments, prepaid commercial instruments, physical commodities — within months of the operation
Threat actor uses layered conventional accounts, often across multiple jurisdictions, to break the audit trail between operational receipt and threat actor's primary financial position

Threat actor's lifestyle changes in a manner consistent with operational proceeds — vehicle purchases, real-estate acquisition, expanded household consumption — without a documented legitimate income source supporting the new pattern

countermeasures.measure: Coordinate with financial intelligence units and law enforcement on transaction monitoring for known threat actor candidates and accomplices in the post-incident window
countermeasures.limitations: Transaction monitoring depends on financial-system cooperation that varies by jurisdiction; cryptocurrency receipts may bypass conventional monitoring entirely

countermeasures.measure: Apply blockchain forensics tools to operational cryptocurrency receipts to trace through mixers and identify cash-out points, particularly at exchanges with KYC requirements
countermeasures.limitations: Privacy coins (Monero, Zcash) substantially defeat current blockchain forensics; sophisticated threat actors layer mixing across multiple chains and protocols to extend the analytical timeline

countermeasures.measure: Coordinate with international financial enforcement partners where disposition crosses jurisdictional lines, particularly into privacy-tolerant or sanctions-non-cooperating jurisdictions
countermeasures.limitations: International cooperation is constrained by treaty and political considerations; some jurisdictions actively shield operational beneficiaries

countermeasures.measure: Maintain detection capability for lifestyle-change patterns in known threat actor candidates as a long-tail attribution vector, particularly for cases where direct financial trails have been successfully obfuscated
countermeasures.limitations: Lifestyle-change detection requires longitudinal observation and benchmark income data that may not be available; signal-to-noise is low without other tying evidence

response_protocols.trigger: Financial disposition indicators detected post-incident — operational-scale receipt traced, mixing activity observed, lifestyle-change pattern surfaced for a threat actor candidate
response_protocols.action: Coordinate with financial intelligence and law enforcement on transaction analysis. Apply blockchain forensics where cryptocurrency is involved. Document the disposition pattern for inclusion in the threat actor profile. Brief the threat assessment team on financial-attribution status.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Disposition pattern ties to known organized network OR cross-border movement of proceeds initiated.
response_protocols.legal_notes: Financial investigation requires legal-process authorization; coordinate with prosecutors and financial intelligence units before any active investigative step. This guidance does not constitute legal advice. Consult qualified legal counsel for jurisdiction-specific requirements.

response_protocols.trigger: Sustained disposition discipline suggesting organized network or professional operator — multi-jurisdictional layering, privacy-coin migration, sustained lifestyle-change concealment
response_protocols.action: Coordinate with international financial enforcement partners. Maintain longitudinal monitoring of identified threat actor candidates and accomplices. Treat the disposition signature as diagnostic of operational sophistication. Update detection methodology and information-sharing posture based on observed patterns.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Disposition pattern reveals connection to known organized financial network or broader criminal enterprise.
response_protocols.legal_notes: Cross-border financial investigation depends on treaty cooperation and foreign jurisdiction policy; coordinate with international enforcement partners early. This guidance does not constitute legal advice. Consult qualified legal counsel for jurisdiction-specific requirements.

tactics.field_notes: Financial Disposition is the threat actor's handling of money after the operation, falling into three pathways in current practice: receipt (ransom payment, contract payment, extortion proceeds arriving from the victim or sponsor), obfuscation (mixing services, chain hopping, privacy coins, layered conventional accounts that break linkability between operation and beneficiary), and laundering (conversion into forms — real estate, business interests, prepaid cards, physical commodities — that present as legitimate to subsequent inspection). The pathway selected reflects the threat actor's resources, sophistication, and the size of the financial flow. Modern financial forensics on blockchain transactions have become a primary investigative tool, and the sophistication of the threat actor's disposition often determines investigative success: a poorly-mixed cryptocurrency receipt traces in hours; a well-laundered flow may take years to attribute. What an investigator looks for is the seam where the operation's proceeds cross from operational anonymity into legitimate-appearing form — that crossing is where Financial Disposition is most catchable.
observed_contexts: kidnap-for-ransom case where the threat actor's cryptocurrency receipt was traced through three mixing services to a regional exchange with KYC requirements, identifying the cash-out beneficiary within 72 hours

contract operation case where layered conventional accounts across four jurisdictions delayed financial attribution by 18 months, with eventual prosecution depending on a single accomplice's cooperation rather than direct financial tracing

extortion case where the threat actor converted operational proceeds into real estate purchases within four months of the operation, identified through public-records analysis after a lifestyle-change pattern surfaced

[literature: CISA-CONVERGE-2021 — pattern of cyber-physical convergent operations using cryptocurrency for both capability acquisition and post-operation receipt, with disposition sophistication determining investigative success]

ransom case where the threat actor's privacy-coin migration of proceeds substantially defeated blockchain forensics, with attribution achieved only through parallel investigation of accomplice communications

tactics.name: After-Action Assessment
tactics.notes: Adversary evaluation of what worked, what failed, and what must change for future operations. After-Action Assessment is present only for persistent, organized actors with intent to operate again. It closes the Operational Feedback Loop — the output of this tactic feeds directly into Phase 1 Target Development for the next operation. Lone actors and opportunity-based actors typically do not execute this tactic.

indicators.behavior: Threat actor's operational signature in successive operations shows progressive refinement — surveillance footprint reduced, cover construction more thorough, timing more reliable, evidence management tighter
Threat actor incorporates lessons from law enforcement public statements about prior operations into modified methodology in subsequent operations
Threat actor's communications and document recovery from prior operations show deliberate analytical activity — methodology critique, after-action notes, lessons-learned documents
Threat actor's training of new accomplices includes deliberate methodology transfer reflecting prior-operation learning, identifiable through accomplice testimony or recovered training materials
Threat actor's operational tempo accelerates or decelerates in patterns consistent with deliberate planning cycles rather than opportunity-driven operation

countermeasures.measure: Maintain longitudinal threat actor tracking across operations to identify methodology evolution that signals organized after-action assessment
countermeasures.limitations: Longitudinal tracking requires sustained analyst attention, jurisdictional authority for cross-case investigation, and sufficient case volume to detect evolution patterns

countermeasures.measure: Manage public statements about operational methodology carefully — public disclosure of detection methods provides the threat actor's after-action assessment with direct intelligence input
countermeasures.limitations: Operational secrecy must be balanced against public accountability and legitimate transparency expectations; over-redaction erodes public trust

countermeasures.measure: Establish information-sharing with law enforcement and intelligence partners on adversary methodology evolution to enable detection of post-AAR refinements before they are operationally deployed
countermeasures.limitations: Information-sharing depth depends on classification, jurisdictional authority, and partner relationships; methodology evolution may outpace sharing cycles

countermeasures.measure: Maintain detection methodology evolution at a tempo that matches or exceeds adversary AAR cycles — defensive learning must not lag offensive learning
countermeasures.limitations: Defensive evolution is constrained by funding, training, and institutional inertia; threat actors with focused resources can outpace defensive cycles in narrow operational lanes

response_protocols.trigger: Methodology evolution detected across linked threat actor operations — signature refinement, cover improvement, tactical adaptation pattern
response_protocols.action: Document the evolution. Update the threat actor profile with current operational signature. Coordinate with intelligence-sharing partners on the observed adaptation. Brief the threat assessment team on detection-methodology gaps revealed by the evolution. Adjust detection posture for subsequent operations.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Evolution pattern indicates capability or organizational expansion OR ties to other open investigations.
response_protocols.legal_notes: Cross-case methodology analysis requires investigative authority across the linked operations; coordinate with prosecutors on case-linking thresholds. This guidance does not constitute legal advice. Consult qualified legal counsel for jurisdiction-specific requirements.

response_protocols.trigger: Recovered AAR materials in post-incident forensic discovery — methodology critique documents, lessons-learned notes, training materials transferred to accomplices
response_protocols.action: Coordinate forensic recovery under chain-of-custody discipline. Brief the threat assessment team on the documented methodology. Cross-reference against current detection capability to identify gaps. Update training and detection posture based on recovered AAR content.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: AAR materials reveal capability or organizational scope beyond the immediate operation.
response_protocols.legal_notes: Recovered documents are evidence subject to chain-of-custody; coordinate with prosecutors before any analysis or sharing that may prejudice prosecution. This guidance does not constitute legal advice. Consult qualified legal counsel for jurisdiction-specific requirements.

tactics.field_notes: After-Action Assessment is the threat actor's evaluation of what worked, what failed, and what must change — applied to future operation planning, false-flag maintenance, deniability preservation, or simply to learn from the operation regardless of any decision about future activity. The operation just completed produced lessons — what worked, what nearly failed, what was observable that shouldn't have been, what surveillance signature the team did not anticipate — and a persistent threat actor extracts those lessons and applies them where useful. This tactic is most prominent for organized actors with operational tempo; lone actors who do not anticipate further activity may skip it, while lone actors under continued investigation pressure often perform it implicitly through cover maintenance. The output of After-Action Assessment is not directly observable in most cases — there's no document or transmission that an investigator can intercept — but its effects appear later: the surveillance signature that was visible last time is absent, the cover story that fell apart under questioning is replaced with a more plausible one, the timing window that was exploited but barely is replaced with a more reliable alternative. What an analyst looks for is the operational evolution of repeat threat actors: each cycle of activity should reveal a tighter, less-observable pattern, and that tightening is the signature of After-Action Assessment in practice.
observed_contexts: transnational organized case where successive kidnapping operations showed progressive surveillance-footprint reduction across three years, identified retrospectively through cross-operation pattern analysis
extremist case where recovered training materials at a captured safe house documented explicit lessons-learned from a prior operation, including detection-method critique and methodology updates

insider-conspirator case where the threat actor's communications during planning of a second operation referenced specific failures from a prior operation and the methodology adaptations being applied

[literature: NTAC-SYSTEMS-2020 — pattern of methodology evolution across linked threat actor operations, with after-action assessment identified as the mechanism producing detection-resistance over time]

professional operator case where the threat actor's pattern across five operations over a decade showed continuous tightening of operational signature, with each cycle producing fewer recoverable artifacts than the prior

tactics.name: Attribution Declaration
tactics.notes: Actor claims responsibility for the operation — communiqué, propaganda release, manifesto delivery, media contact, or direct communication to authorities. Attribution declaration is the defining behavior of terrorists, ideologically motivated actors, and extortionists. The claim is the communicative act that converts physical violence into political or social leverage.

indicators.behavior: Threat actor releases a written communiqué, manifesto, or video statement claiming responsibility for the operation through any public or semi-public channel
Threat actor contacts media organizations directly with attribution claims, supporting documentation, or operational details that confirm insider knowledge
Threat actor releases pre-recorded attribution material — manifesto video, statement document — to multiple platforms simultaneously to defeat takedown and maximize reach
Threat actor communicates attribution directly to the targeted subject's organization, family, or law enforcement with operational demands or leverage assertions

Threat actor remains silent on attribution despite political incentive to claim responsibility, indicating either operational discipline (network protection priority) or deliberate third-party attribution misdirection

Threat actor's affiliated group or parent organization issues the attribution claim rather than the threat actor directly, with the threat actor either confirming through subsequent communication or remaining silent to preserve operational deniability

countermeasures.measure: Coordinate with media organizations and platform providers on rapid takedown of attribution materials that violate platform policy or cross into incitement of further violence
countermeasures.limitations: Takedown is reactive and slower than initial reach; sophisticated threat actors pre-distribute material across multiple platforms to defeat single-platform takedown

countermeasures.measure: Maintain forensic capability to authenticate or invalidate attribution claims — voice analysis, document forensics, metadata examination — to defeat misdirection attempts
countermeasures.limitations: Attribution forensics requires specialized expertise; sophisticated threat actors can produce material designed to defeat current authentication methods

countermeasures.measure: Coordinate public-information posture with law enforcement to avoid amplifying the threat actor's intended message while still providing accurate factual information to affected communities
countermeasures.limitations: Information control during active investigation must balance operational security against legitimate public transparency expectations

countermeasures.measure: Establish information-sharing with intelligence partners on attribution claims to detect false-flag or third-party-misdirection attempts and identify pattern matches across cases
countermeasures.limitations: Attribution analysis depends on cross-case data and signature recognition; novel attribution methods may not match prior patterns

response_protocols.trigger: Attribution declaration received during or immediately after incident — communiqué, manifesto, video statement, or direct media contact
response_protocols.action: Activate attribution-response protocols. Coordinate with law enforcement on authentication. Initiate platform-takedown coordination if material crosses policy thresholds. Apply public-information discipline to avoid amplification while providing accurate factual information. Brief executive leadership and external communications team.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Attribution is authenticated AND ties to known threat group OR contains additional threats requiring protective response.
response_protocols.legal_notes: Attribution material may be evidence subject to chain-of-custody; coordinate with prosecutors before any analysis or sharing. Platform takedown decisions may carry First Amendment or jurisdictional implications. This guidance does not constitute legal advice. Consult qualified legal counsel for jurisdiction-specific requirements.

response_protocols.trigger: Delayed or third-party attribution claim post-incident — affiliated group claim, manifesto release weeks after the incident, or recovered material containing attribution intent not previously publicized
response_protocols.action: Coordinate authentication with law enforcement. Brief the threat assessment team on the attribution context and threat actor profile implications. Update public-information posture if previously framed as unattributed. Cross-reference against open investigations for pattern matches.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Authenticated attribution reveals expanded organizational involvement OR ties to other open investigations.
response_protocols.legal_notes: Third-party attribution claims must be authenticated before being treated as accurate; affiliated-group claims may not reflect actual operational responsibility. This guidance does not constitute legal advice. Consult qualified legal counsel for jurisdiction-specific requirements.

tactics.field_notes: Attribution Declaration is the moment the threat actor commits the operation to a public political, ideological, or coercive frame. The kinetic event is now complete and the threat actor faces a discrete choice: claim responsibility (and convert physical violence into political or social leverage), deny responsibility (and protect the operational network and personal safety), or remain anonymous (and let the act stand without interpretation). The declaration may be a written communiqué, a manifesto release, a video statement, a media contact, or a direct communication to law enforcement or the targeted subject's organization. For terrorists, ideologically motivated actors, and extortionists, attribution declaration is the operational point — without the claim, the violence does not produce the intended political or coercive effect. For nation-state actors, attribution may be deliberately withheld or fabricated to misdirect blame to a third party. What an analyst observes is the timing, channel, and content of the declaration: who claims, when they claim, what platform they choose, and how the message is framed.
observed_contexts: extremist attack where the threat actor pre-distributed a manifesto across multiple platforms minutes before the kinetic moment, defeating initial takedown and maximizing reach within the first 24 hours
kidnap-for-ransom case where the threat actor delivered attribution to the targeted subject's family privately, declining public claim to preserve negotiation leverage and operational deniability
ideologically motivated case where attribution was claimed by an affiliated group within hours, with the operational lead remaining silent to protect the broader network
[literature: NTAC-MASS-2021 — pattern of pre-recorded attribution material distribution at mass attack cases, including manifesto-platform pre-staging]

nation-state operation where attribution was deliberately constructed to misdirect blame to a third party, identified retrospectively through forensic analysis of message metadata and operational artifacts

tactics.name: Audience Amplification
tactics.notes: Actor maximizes the reach and impact of the attribution message — media exploitation, social platform posting, staged documentation distribution, manipulation of coverage framing. Audience Amplification is the force multiplier for attribution-seeking actors: the operation's communicative impact is proportional to audience reach.
tactics.cpn_notes: Social media platforms, video hosting sites, and encrypted broadcast channels have displaced traditional media as the primary audience amplification channel. Actors with media production capabilities can release high-quality content that drives algorithmic amplification without press contact.

indicators.behavior: Threat actor distributes attribution material across multiple social media platforms simultaneously to maximize reach and defeat platform-by-platform takedown
Threat actor uses encrypted broadcast channels (Telegram, Discord, dark web forums) to seed attribution material to affiliated communities for re-amplification on public platforms
Threat actor produces high-quality media materials — edited video, narrative documents, propaganda graphics — that drive algorithmic amplification independent of press contact
Threat actor's amplification strategy exploits ongoing news cycles, anniversary dates, or related events to maintain sustained visibility beyond the immediate post-incident window
Threat actor coordinates amplification with affiliated networks — sympathizer accounts, shared community pages — to drive engagement metrics that trigger algorithmic recommendation

Threat actor's amplification pattern shifts in response to platform takedown — moving to less-moderated platforms, fragmenting content to defeat detection, or using human re-uploads to evade automated removal

countermeasures.measure: Coordinate with major social media platforms on rapid attribution-material takedown protocols for incidents that meet platform-policy thresholds for violent content or incitement
countermeasures.limitations: Takedown is reactive and content reposts faster than removal; platform policies vary and may not cover all attribution material

countermeasures.measure: Maintain monitoring of secondary and tertiary platforms — encrypted broadcast channels, less-moderated sites — where attribution material migrates after primary-platform takedown
countermeasures.limitations: Secondary-platform monitoring requires sustained analyst attention; encrypted channels may not be visible without legal process or insider access

countermeasures.measure: Apply public-information discipline to incident response that does not amplify the threat actor's intended message while still providing accurate factual information to affected communities
countermeasures.limitations: Public-information balance is judgment-intensive and varies by event type; over-restriction erodes public trust

countermeasures.measure: Coordinate with research and academic partners on tracking algorithmic amplification patterns to inform detection and counter-amplification methodology
countermeasures.limitations: Algorithmic amplification analysis is constrained by platform data access; methodology evolves continuously and academic cycles may lag operational tempo

response_protocols.trigger: Attribution material distribution detected during incident or immediate post-incident period
response_protocols.action: Activate platform-takedown coordination. Apply public-information discipline. Monitor secondary and tertiary platforms for migration. Coordinate with law enforcement on authentication and attribution analysis. Brief executive leadership and external communications team.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Distribution scale exceeds rapid takedown capacity OR material includes additional threats requiring protective response.
response_protocols.legal_notes: Platform takedown decisions may carry First Amendment or jurisdictional implications; coordinate with legal before any unilateral action. This guidance does not constitute legal advice. Consult qualified legal counsel for jurisdiction-specific requirements.

response_protocols.trigger: Sustained amplification activity through secondary platforms after primary takedown — encrypted broadcast channels, dark web forums, alt-platform reposts
response_protocols.action: Maintain longitudinal monitoring of identified amplification networks. Coordinate with law enforcement on legal-process pathways for closed-platform investigation. Update detection methodology based on observed migration patterns. Brief intelligence-sharing partners on signature recognition.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Amplification pattern reveals connection to known organized network or ongoing operational activity.
response_protocols.legal_notes: Closed-platform investigation requires legal-process authorization; coordinate with prosecutors and platform legal teams before any active investigative step. This guidance does not constitute legal advice. Consult qualified legal counsel for jurisdiction-specific requirements.

tactics.field_notes: Audience Amplification is the threat actor's deliberate maximization of the attribution message's reach and impact. The operation has produced violence and the attribution declaration has produced a frame; Audience Amplification converts that frame into ongoing political, social, or coercive leverage by ensuring the largest possible audience receives it in the form the threat actor intends. Modern threat actors increasingly bypass traditional media: social media platforms, video hosting services, encrypted broadcast channels, and algorithm-driven recommendation systems allow direct distribution of attribution material at scale and speed that previously required institutional gatekeepers. For ideological and extortion-motivated actors, amplification is the force multiplier — the operation's communicative impact is proportional to audience reach, and a successfully amplified attribution claim can produce political effects far in excess of the kinetic act itself. What an analyst observes during Audience Amplification is the distribution pattern: which platforms, what timing, what supporting media, what algorithmic cues the threat actor exploits to drive engagement.
observed_contexts: extremist attack where the threat actor pre-distributed a manifesto video across six platforms simultaneously, defeating initial takedown and reaching an estimated audience of millions in the first 48 hours

ideologically motivated case where coordinated affiliated-network amplification drove the attribution material to algorithmic recommendation, sustaining visibility for weeks despite primary-platform takedown
extortion case where the threat actor amplified attribution through encrypted broadcast channels seeded with sympathizer communities, generating sustained pressure on the targeted organization
[literature: CISA-CONVERGE-2021 — pattern of cyber-physical convergent amplification using social media and encrypted channels to maximize ideological-attack communicative impact]
domestic terrorism case where the threat actor's amplification strategy exploited a related news cycle weeks after the incident, returning the case to public attention and pressuring policy response

tactics.name: Coercive Leverage
tactics.notes: Actor makes direct contact with the victim, victim's family, or relevant decision-makers to assert leverage — ransom demand, negotiation, proof-of-life, threat escalation, and deadline management. Coercive Leverage requires the actor to have achieved a position of power (captive, stolen asset, credible threat) and now converts that position into a demand.

indicators.behavior: Threat actor makes direct contact with the victim's family, employer, government agency, or other decision-maker to assert leverage and articulate demands

Threat actor provides proof-of-life — recorded video of the captive with current-event reference, fingerprint or biometric submission, recorded voice with date confirmation — to validate the leverage position
Threat actor articulates specific demands with deadlines and consequences for non-compliance — ransom amount, prisoner release, policy change, financial disposition
Threat actor escalates threats over time — increasing severity, accelerating deadlines, demonstrating capability — to pressure decision-makers toward compliance
Threat actor's communications during leverage phase show negotiation framing, demand evolution, and willingness to test various pressure paths to identify the most compliance-likely target

Threat actor uses third-party intermediaries — religious figures, community leaders, or traditional intermediaries — as channels for demand transmission, exploiting their access while constraining direct attribution

countermeasures.measure: Coordinate with law enforcement on crisis-negotiation deployment for incidents involving sustained leverage scenarios — ransom demand, hostage situation, extortion threat
countermeasures.limitations: Crisis-negotiation effectiveness varies by jurisdiction and case type; some leverage scenarios resolve only through tactical intervention rather than negotiation

countermeasures.measure: Maintain proof-of-life and proof-of-leverage authentication capability — voice analysis, video forensics, biometric verification — to detect fabrication attempts and validate genuine leverage positions
countermeasures.limitations: Authentication forensics requires specialized expertise; sophisticated threat actors can fabricate proof material that defeats current verification methods

countermeasures.measure: Establish family liaison and decision-maker preparation protocols including non-disclosure of negotiation status and information-control during the leverage window
countermeasures.limitations: Information control during emotional family pressure is difficult to maintain; media inquiry and social-media leakage can compromise negotiation posture

countermeasures.measure: Coordinate with international counterparts where leverage scenarios involve cross-border movement of captives, demands, or beneficiaries
countermeasures.limitations: International coordination is constrained by treaty and political considerations; some jurisdictions actively shield operational beneficiaries

response_protocols.trigger: Coercive leverage assertion received with active leverage position — captive held, sensitive material withheld, credible threat of recurrence
response_protocols.action: Activate full crisis-management response. Coordinate hostage-negotiation team or extortion-response team deployment. Authenticate leverage claims (proof-of-life, proof-of-material). Activate family liaison and information-control protocols. Brief executive leadership and legal. Document the demand articulation and deadline structure contemporaneously.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Time-sensitive demands with credible threat of harm OR multi-victim leverage OR cross-jurisdictional demand structure.
response_protocols.legal_notes: Leverage scenarios trigger jurisdiction-specific crisis-negotiation authority and tactical-intervention thresholds; coordination with law enforcement on use-of-force authority and negotiation strategy is mandatory. This guidance does not constitute legal advice. Consult qualified legal counsel for jurisdiction-specific requirements.

response_protocols.trigger: Sustained leverage scenario requiring multi-day negotiation management — extended hostage situation, prolonged extortion campaign, ongoing demand escalation
response_protocols.action: Maintain crisis-management posture across multiple operational periods. Conduct negotiation strategy reviews at each shift change. Coordinate authentication of every escalation claim. Maintain family liaison continuity. Prepare for possible tactical intervention pending negotiation outcome.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Negotiation breakdown OR threat-credibility increase OR threat actor demonstrates capability to act on escalating threats.
response_protocols.legal_notes: Multi-day crisis management carries jurisdiction-specific authorities and obligations including notification to higher levels of government in some cases. Coordinate with legal continuously throughout the scenario. This guidance does not constitute legal advice. Consult qualified legal counsel for jurisdiction-specific requirements.

tactics.field_notes: By the time Coercive Leverage is observable, the threat actor has converted operational success into ongoing demand: the targeted subject is held captive, sensitive information has been extracted, or a credible threat of recurrence has been established, and the threat actor now uses that position to extract concessions from the victim's family, employer, government, or affiliated decision-makers. The leverage may be physical (a held hostage), informational (proof-of-life paired with extortion threat), positional (occupied facility with hostages or sensitive material), or threat-based (credible promise of further violence absent compliance). Coercive Leverage requires sustained operational tempo: the threat actor must maintain the leverage condition — captive remains held, information remains unreleased, threat remains credible — while simultaneously extracting concessions. What an analyst observes during Coercive Leverage is the demand articulation: the timing of contacts, the channel chosen, the form of proof-of-life or proof-of-leverage, the deadline structure, and the threat escalation path used to compel compliance.
observed_contexts: kidnap-for-ransom case where coercive leverage was sustained across eleven days, with the threat actor cycling demand articulation through three intermediaries before final resolution via cryptocurrency payment

extortion case where the threat actor maintained credible threat-based leverage against a corporate decision-maker over six months, using staged escalation incidents to demonstrate capability without crossing into operational triggers
hostage incident where rapid crisis-negotiation deployment authenticated proof-of-life within four hours and managed a 36-hour negotiation to peaceful resolution

In aftermath leverage, the actor's demands typically come in sequence with deadlines attached — specific demand sequences, time pressure, escalation triggers that shape the crisis-negotiation team's posture from the first contact

transnational case where coercive leverage was applied through religious-figure intermediary to a foreign government, identified retrospectively when the intermediary disclosed the threat actor's instructions during post-resolution debriefing

person.scope: Tactics centered on one or more human beings as the primary target. The adversary's primary objective is harm, control, coercion, or surveillance directed at people. Setting and motivation are separate dimensions and do not change matrix placement.

facility.scope: Tactics centered on a physical venue, structure, or built environment as the primary target. The adversary's primary objective is damage, destruction, denial, or symbolic action against the place itself. Incidental human harm in an unoccupied facility does not move the tactic to People.

organization.scope: Tactics centered on an institution, mission, brand, or operational continuity as the primary target. The adversary's primary objective is disruption, delegitimization, infiltration, or coercion of what the organization does or represents, distinct from its facilities or its individuals.

infrastructure.scope: Tactics centered on infrastructure or technical systems as the primary target. The adversary's primary objective is disruption, degradation, or compromise of the system's function — physical infrastructure, cyber-physical systems, or critical service delivery. Cyber-Physical Nexus tactics are tagged via the cpn field on tactic.

actor_profiles.name: Fixated Individual
actor_profiles.description: Psychologically-driven actor with obsessive focus on a specific named target. The fixation is the defining characteristic — this actor's threat is organized entirely around one person. Motivation is personal, delusional, or grievance-rooted. Follows a slow-building predatory pathway that may span months to years. Clinical anchor: WAVR-21, PATH model, Threat Assessment in Schools.
behavioral_markers: Sustained surveillance or contact attempts directed at one specific named target
Leakage of fixation content to third parties — friends, family, online platforms
Escalating attempts to communicate with or approach the target despite rejection
Acquisition of the target's personal information, schedule, and location patterns
Grievance documentation — letters, journals, social media posts referencing the target

actor_profiles.name: Domestic / Intimate Partner
actor_profiles.description: Actor in or formerly in an intimate, family, or cohabiting relationship with the target. The prior relationship is both the access vector and the motivational anchor. Distinct from the Fixated Individual — the pathway is rooted in control, jealousy, or retaliation rather than obsessive attachment from a distance. Covers intimate partner violence, domestic homicide, stalking by former partners, and family-based violence.
behavioral_markers: Prior or current intimate/family relationship with the target
History of controlling, coercive, or threatening behavior within the relationship
Violation of protective or restraining orders
Monitoring of target's location, communications, and social relationships
Escalation following separation, divorce proceedings, or custody disputes

actor_profiles.name: Crisis-Driven
actor_profiles.description: Individual actor whose pathway to violence is precipitated by an identifiable personal crisis — job loss, financial ruin, relationship breakdown, mental health episode, or a desire for notoriety and legacy. Unlike the Fixated Individual, the target is often symbolic or opportunistic rather than a specific named person. The crisis compresses Phase 1 dramatically: the window from ideation to action may be days or weeks, not months. The notoriety-seeking dimension connects this actor type to attribution-seeking Phase 4 behavior even without ideological content.
behavioral_markers: Identifiable precipitating crisis event immediately preceding behavioral change
Rapid deterioration in work performance, relationships, or personal stability
Leakage of intent — often to multiple people, sometimes publicly
Language expressing desire to be known, remembered, or understood
Target selection based on symbolic representation of the grievance source, not personal relationship

actor_profiles.name: Malicious Insider
actor_profiles.description: Current employee, contractor, or trusted-access holder who deliberately exploits their legitimate access to harm the organization, its people, or its assets. The trust relationship is the attack surface. Motivation may be grievance-based, financially motivated, or ideological. Phase 1 is compressed because the actor is already inside — they know the target, the layout, the security gaps, and the personnel.
behavioral_markers: Observable behavioral deterioration — withdrawal, hostility, policy violations
Anomalous access patterns — systems, locations, or data outside their operational need
Unexplained external contact establishment or suspicious external relationships
Acquisition of materials inconsistent with job role (portable storage, recording equipment)
Testing organizational response to minor violations to calibrate detection capability

actor_profiles.name: Coerced Insider
actor_profiles.description: Current trusted-access holder who is being blackmailed, threatened, or otherwise coerced into facilitating an attack or intelligence collection operation. The actor knows what they are doing but is not acting freely. Coercion may be based on personal compromising information, threats to family, or financial leverage. Detection is complicated because the actor's outward grievance indicators are suppressed — they appear compliant rather than hostile.
behavioral_markers: Sudden behavioral change without apparent internal grievance — anxiety, hypervigilance, social withdrawal
Unexplained financial pressure or sudden resolution of financial problems
Unusual communications security behaviors — new devices, encrypted apps, changed routines
Compliance with unusual external requests without pushback or documentation
Reluctance to discuss personal life; possible indicators of external surveillance of the actor themselves

actor_profiles.name: Recruited Insider
actor_profiles.description: Current trusted-access holder who has been deliberately recruited by an external actor — typically a state intelligence service, organized criminal group, or competitor — and is willingly cooperating. Unlike the coerced insider, this actor chose the relationship. They are disciplined, operationally patient, and actively work to expand their access and preserve their position. Among the hardest insider threat profiles to detect.
behavioral_markers: Sustained covert relationship with an external handler, often disguised as a professional or personal contact
Deliberate access scope expansion beyond their operational role over time
Disciplined information aggregation across systems and people without triggering individual alarms
Unexplained affluence or financial activity inconsistent with salary
High operational security — carefully manages evidence trail, may generate false audit records

actor_profiles.name: Negligent Insider
actor_profiles.description: Current trusted-access holder who creates risk through carelessness, poor security hygiene, or disregard for policy — without intent to cause harm. Not a threat actor in the traditional sense, but a significant risk vector. The negligent insider is frequently the entry point exploited by external actors. Susceptibility to social engineering and phishing is the primary mechanism.
behavioral_markers: Repeated security policy violations without apparent concern for consequences
Susceptibility to social engineering attempts — shares passwords, follows unauthorized instructions
Ignores escalating warning signals or security notifications
Uses personal devices or unsecured channels for sensitive work
Does not report suspicious contacts or requests from unknown parties

actor_profiles.name: Unwitting Insider
actor_profiles.description: Current trusted-access holder who is being exploited by an external actor without their knowledge. Their normal work behavior is the delivery mechanism. They may provide access, information, or physical proximity that they believe is routine. Detection requires identifying the external actor doing the exploiting — the insider's behavior appears normal because it is normal from their perspective. A state intelligence service using a foreign business contact as an unwitting collection platform is the archetype.
behavioral_markers: From the insider's perspective: normal behavior — no behavioral indicators present
Detection pathway: identify the external actor, then map who they have access to
May be approached under a professional or personal pretext with no indication of intelligence purpose
The exploiting actor manages the relationship to keep the insider unaware
Post-detection: insider is typically a victim/witness, not a prosecutorial target

actor_profiles.name: Opportunistic Criminal
actor_profiles.description: Financially motivated actor with minimal planning who exploits available opportunity. Target is selected based on perceived vulnerability, not advance research. Low operational sophistication and low operational security — evidence trail is typically recoverable. Violence is instrumental and proportional to perceived resistance. Acts quickly on available conditions rather than waiting for optimal timing.
behavioral_markers: Target selection based on visible vulnerability — unlocked vehicle, isolated pedestrian, unattended property
Minimal pre-attack preparation or reconnaissance
Low operational security — no counter-surveillance behavior
Improvised capability — uses whatever is at hand
Pattern of escalation from minor offenses toward more serious crimes

actor_profiles.name: Professional Criminal
actor_profiles.description: Financially motivated actor operating as a hired professional — assassin, kidnap-for-ransom specialist, security contractor operating outside legal bounds. Executes for payment, not ideology. Applies professional tradecraft: pre-operational surveillance, covert capability acquisition, practiced withdrawal. Full phase completion is the operational norm. Distinguishable from organized criminal enterprise by individual or small-team structure and contract-based operation.
behavioral_markers: Pre-operational surveillance of target using professional counter-detection methods
Covert capability acquisition through channels that obscure the procurement trail
No ideological or personal connection to the target — purely transactional
Systematic withdrawal and evidence management post-operation
Financial transaction pattern consistent with contracted payment receipt

actor_profiles.name: Organized Criminal Group
actor_profiles.description: Enterprise-level criminal organization with division of roles, financial infrastructure, and operational capacity spanning multiple operations. Cartel, syndicate, or organized crime network. Kidnap-for-ransom, extortion, trafficking, and targeted violence against rivals or witnesses are primary THREAT-relevant operations. Uses cutouts, intermediaries, and financial layering. Phase 4 Financial Disposition is a defining operational capability.
behavioral_markers: Multiple actors with compartmented and specialized roles
Financial infrastructure for receiving and laundering proceeds
Use of cutouts and intermediaries to separate principals from operations
Established communications security and counter-surveillance protocols
Pattern of prior incidents establishing organizational TTPs

actor_profiles.name: Corporate Spy
actor_profiles.description: Actor focused on covert intelligence collection — stealing trade secrets, IP, client data, strategic plans, or personnel information for delivery to a competitor, state actor, or criminal purchaser. The defining operational logic is preservation of access: unlike the saboteur, the corporate spy wants to keep going back. Stealth and access maintenance are primary operational values. May be an insider acting on behalf of an external principal or an external actor who has gained insider access through recruitment or social engineering.
behavioral_markers: Covert access to sensitive data or systems beyond their operational role
Aggregation of information across multiple systems and people in a pattern inconsistent with job function
Deliberate concealment of information collection activities — after-hours access, personal devices
Sustained contact with an external handler disguised as professional or personal relationship
Deliberate preservation of access — avoids triggering reviews, maintains low profile

actor_profiles.name: Industrial Saboteur
actor_profiles.description: Actor focused on physically destroying or disabling operational capability — machinery, production systems, infrastructure, or records. Unlike the corporate spy, the saboteur's operation is consumptive: the objective is to break something, not take something. May be grievance-driven, state-directed, competitor-directed, or ideologically motivated. Timing around business-critical events (product launch, merger, regulatory deadline) is a characteristic indicator. Uses legitimate access to reach systems that would otherwise require forced entry.
behavioral_markers: Access to operational or physical systems beyond normal job function
Unexplained presence near critical equipment, infrastructure nodes, or safety systems
Evidence of tampering with machinery, processes, or safety controls
Timing correlation with business-critical events or organizational stress periods
May disguise access as maintenance, inspection, or contractor activity

actor_profiles.name: Issue-Oriented Activist
actor_profiles.description: Ideologically motivated actor whose goal is exposure, embarrassment, disruption, or policy change — not physical harm to people. Physical harm to persons is actively avoided because it would undermine the message. Property damage and operational disruption are within scope. Attribution is essential — the claim is the point. Operates in a legal-to-illegal spectrum that makes early intervention difficult. Distinguishable from terrorist by the absence of mass casualty intent and the communicative primacy of the non-violent message.
behavioral_markers: Public organizing activity, social media coordination, and recruitment visible before the action
Targets selected for symbolic or operational significance to the cause, not for maximum casualties
Prior incidents of civil disobedience or low-level property disruption in the pattern
Strong attribution-seeking behavior — prepared statements, media contacts, livestreaming
Avoidance of methods likely to cause human casualties

actor_profiles.name: Saboteur
actor_profiles.description: Ideologically motivated actor whose goal is the destruction or disabling of infrastructure or operational capability. Physical harm to people is acceptable, not the primary objective. Targets are selected for their operational significance — pipelines, power nodes, water systems, communications infrastructure. May operate as a lone actor or in a small cell. Attribution is conditional: environmental or anti-state saboteurs may claim credit; state-affiliated saboteurs typically do not.
behavioral_markers: Reconnaissance of infrastructure targets — substations, pipelines, pumping stations, communication towers
Acquisition of destructive materials — explosives, incendiaries, or tools for physical tampering
Operational security behaviors suggesting awareness of surveillance
Target selection pattern focused on operational chokepoints and high-consequence nodes
May conduct Partial Approach Rehearsal at target sites across multiple days

actor_profiles.name: Terrorist
actor_profiles.description: Ideologically or politically motivated actor who uses violence as a communicative instrument — to coerce policy, shape public perception, or demonstrate capability. The violence is not the end; it is the message. Attribution is operationally required: terrorism without a claim loses its coercive power. Target selection is based on symbolic value or policy leverage, not maximum casualty efficiency. Organized cells apply full phase completion. Lone terrorists may compress Phase 1 based on radicalization timeline.
behavioral_markers: Ideological radicalization indicators — consumption of extremist content, rhetoric escalation, community withdrawal
Operational security behaviors — encrypted communications, new devices, changed routines
Target selection research focused on symbolic value or media visibility
Capability acquisition for mass-casualty or high-impact methods
Phase 4 attribution is mandatory — prepared communiqués, media contacts, or symbolic claim delivery

actor_profiles.name: Violent Extremist
actor_profiles.description: Ideologically motivated actor for whom causing mass harm or death is the operational end, not merely the instrument. Distinct from the terrorist — coercion is not the goal; elimination or destruction of the target group is. Attribution may be claimed or implicit but is not operationally required. Mass casualty capacity is the capability selection criterion. May exhibit martyrdom posture in Phase 4 — no evasion planning, active engagement with responders, or suicide by cop.
behavioral_markers: Escalating dehumanization of a target group in communications and expressed ideology
Leakage of eliminationist language — destruction, annihilation, cleansing rhetoric
Acquisition of mass-casualty capable methods — firearms, explosives, vehicles
Target selection based on demographic density of the target group, not symbolic value
Martyrdom posture — no withdrawal planning, final communications framed as legacy

actor_profiles.name: State Actor
actor_profiles.description: Nation-state directed, sponsored, or sanctioned adversary operating with the full intelligence apparatus of a state — collection, planning support, logistics, and exfiltration infrastructure. Deniability architecture is a Phase 1 planning input, not an afterthought. Highest capability across all matrices. May use proxy actors. Operations span all four matrices simultaneously for complex targets. Full phase completion is the norm; Phase 1 may extend over months with parallel Phase 2 preparation.
behavioral_markers: Professional counter-surveillance and surveillance detection routines throughout all phases
Multi-actor team with compartmented roles and need-to-know discipline
Access to sophisticated capability — specialized tools, forged documents, sterile communications
Pre-planned withdrawal with assets positioned before operation initiation
Deniability architecture visible in how the operation is structured and what is left behind

actor_profiles.name: State-Sponsored Actor
actor_profiles.description: Actor funded, directed, or enabled by a state intelligence service while maintaining a non-state appearance — contractor, criminal organization, hacktivist front, or private intelligence firm operating with state backing. Witting of the state relationship. The sponsoring state gains operational capability with plausible deniability. Distinct from State Actor (direct operation) — the sponsoring relationship adds a layer that complicates attribution and legal accountability.
behavioral_markers: Operates with resources and capability inconsistent with apparent organizational size or revenue
Access to state-grade intelligence products and tradecraft without apparent state affiliation
Operations align with sponsoring state's geopolitical interests or target lists
Financial flows from obscured state-affiliated sources
